speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In connection with a petition which I presented to the House of Commons, protesting against immigration, the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 1, 1939, in an article headed " Muddying Welcome on Canada's Mat," used the following expressions with regard to my race and myself:
The experience of the Canadian Indians has been exceptional. Mr. Wilfrid Lacroix of Quebec-Montmorency should try to remember that fact, suppress his ancestral consciousness of guilt and approach the problems of to-day and Canada's part in their solution, not as a robber bent on holding his spoils from other robbers, but as a civilized man charged with a civilized man's duty to civilization. . . .
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to remind the publisher of the Globe and Mail that he is totally ignorant of Canada's history, for, had he opened its finest pages, he would have noted the obscure heroism of our early evangelists and missionaries, such as the Reverend Jesuit Fathers and others who, by dint of persuasion and unparalleled personal sacrifices and aided by brave colonists whom I am proud to own as my ancestors opened this vast continent to Christianity and civilization.
Long before the ancestors of the publisher of the Globe and Mail landed in this country, my forefathers had by their gigantic labours already made it a nation. And if he will accompany me to the old cemeteries of Quebec province he will find inscribed there names of which Canadian history is proud.
The publisher of the Globe and Mail having dared to compare the members of my race to robbers, I am compelled to remind him that those who made the most brilliant contribution to our confederation, which permits us to sit here to-day, are Canadians of French origin.

Bren Gun-Mr. Manion
May I also remind the publisher of the Globe and Mail that those who defended with the greatest tenacity against the Americans at the battle of Quebec, the last parcel of British territory left on this north American continent, were French Canadians, many of his ancestors having fled the city.
Allow me to tell him also that by writing such nonsense the Globe and Mail is not working for unity in this country and that if his paper has any honour it will retract its words.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, February 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Neil:
That the agreement between the government and the John Inglis Company, of Toronto, for the manufacture of Bren machine guns, the report of the royal commission dealing with said agreement, and all related documents, evidence, vouchers and exhibits, be referred to the standing committee on public accounts.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
On Friday last the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke on this question at some length. He discussed the report in a general way and I intend to do likewise.
With one of his remarks, to the effect that in appointing Mr. Justice Davis he was sure he had selected as commissioner one who would be satisfactory to the country, I am in complete accord. Mr. Justice Davis without doubt was satisfactory to all. His reputation is of the highest, I entirely agree with the Prime Minister that he could not have chosen anyone more satisfactory unless it were the chief justice himself; and indeed I think that Mr. Justice Davis was just as satisfactory as the chief justice himself would have been in that case.
The Prime Minister mentioned the fact that Mr. Justice Davis had been appointed to the bench by our party. That I think was hardly necessary, because I believe that gener-71492-II
ally speaking, the judges of the higher courts of Canada whichever side appoints them, are honourable and entirely beyond partisanship after their appointment to the bench.
The Prime Minister's speech seems to me to show the need of discussion of this question here in the House of Commons, not by a committee such as the standing committee on public accounts. The Prime Minister referred to an expression I used some days ago somewhat hurriedly, the term "packed committee." As I said at the time, I used the expression in no offensive sense. What I meant was that that committee, composed as it is under the rules of the house of fifty members, would consist of eight members of our party, three of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and three of the Social Credit party-that is, fourteen representing all the different opposition parties to thirty-six on the government side. A committee made up in these proportions, as it would be under the rules, is likely to be a little more partisan than is the House of Commons itself, because in committees party feeling runs strongly; it always has. At the moment I do not recall any public accounts committee, set up in the manner in which this has been set up, bringing in any report against the government of the day. What I really mean is that the committee would be so overwhelmingly of one party that there would not be the same freedom of discussion as there is in this house.
One thing in the Prime Minister's speech to which I think I should take exception was the reference to a rule affecting any special committee that might be set up. He pointed out that if it were a special committee instead of a standing committee, there is a rule which provides that if hon. members commit themselves strongly on one side they should not be appointed as members of the committee. That is correct in reference to a special committee, but, as pointed out by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), it does not refer to a standing committee. Although I did not think of the same word as that used by my hon. friend, "intimidation," the thought ran through my mind that the reference made by the Prime Minister in that regard might rather tend to frighten all of us, and particularly those in the opposition sections, from free participation in the discussions. I thought it a little unfortunate that the Prime Minister should have made that reference, because the rule does not refer to a standing committee. It is true that any special committee might later

Bren Gun-Mr. Manion

be turned into a standing committee, but as the committee stands at present the rule does not apply to it.
The anxiety of the Prime Minister and the government as a whole-although they made no fight for it-to have this question passed to the standing committee at once, without discussion, struck me as more or less indicative of a desire to bury the whole report. After all, this question has been investigated by a commissioner, who, we all agree, is an outstanding man. There were counsel for the various parties; the government had three counsel, there was counsel for the Inglis company, including Mr. Hahn; counsel for Cameron, Pointon & Merritt, and Mr. Plaxton, counsel for the Maclean Publishing Company and Colonel Drew. So there were plenty of counsel. The commission sat for over two months and the cost was over ? 15.000. There is every reason for believing that the matter was so thoroughly investigated that it would not appear to be necessary for a committee of the house again to go over the whole matter.

That was up to the first of February; so it was a fairly expensive investigation, although the Prime Minister tells us neither Mr. Justice Davis nor Colonel Ralston took anything for themselves. We have before us the report, made after very full investigation; therefore I ask why the report should be submitted to a committee, whatever committee	it may	be,	with theheavy expense involved for the calling of witnesses again and going over the same ground, a rehashing of the same matters in dispute. It seems to me that parliament is the forum	to deal	with it.	The	report isnow submitted to the jury of this parliament, and	through	this parliament to the
people of Canada whom we represent.
I repeat	that in	view of	all	the facts
this is the place to discuss the whole question. Therefore I am opposed in a general way, I regret to say, to the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Mac-Neil). His speech in the debate on the address, in which he reviewed the whole Bren gun question, was a splendid effort, to my mind one of the best and most effective speeches I have heard in this house. But his motion does not strike me as the preferable way of dealing with the matter at this time.

Now to deal with the report itself. When it first came out, indeed before it was made public, information was given through the press, I do not know by whom, that the report was a complete exoneration of the government in so far as the Bren gun contract was concerned. To my mind that was merely propaganda. Far from this report being a complete exoneration of the government and those associated with the giving of this contract, it seems to me it is a complete condemnation of the government, as I shall prove before I finish. It is true that there was no evidence of corruption, but no one had charged corruption. I do not charge anything in the way of corruption now. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) quoted from page 51 of the report, where Mr. Justice Davis eliminated anything in the way of any suspicion of corruption. I accept that; far be it from me to suggest anything to the contrary. But, sir, there are fifty-two pages in this report, and I venture to say that on at least forty of them there is an absolute condemnation of the minister and, through him, of the government for having made this contract at all.
I say that Mr. Justice Davis, for reasons with which I shall deal briefly, felt that he could not come out and say distinctly that he condemned the minister or the government; he did exonerate them, of course, from anything in the nature of corruption. But in dealing with the methods by which the contract was put into effect he could not come out frankly and say what he thought, because of the arguments placed before him by various counsel, including government counsel, so he did it in a sort of subtle manner, by painting vignettes which he hung on the wall for each of us to see and come to his own conclusion.
After reading this blue book I should say that Mr. Justice Davis is an author of distinction. In many ways it is a little classic, a most fascinating, interesting and well-done booklet. But it has just a touch of subtlety so that one has to study it a bit to see exactly what Mr. Justice Davis means. Once one has read it, however, as I intend to read a few selections from it to-day, I think what Mr. Justice Davis had in the back of his mind but does not express in the booklet is so clear that one needs very little imagination to understand at what he is pointing. Indeed, sir, I think you could open this book almost at random and find that it condemns-by inference-the method by which this contract was negotiated. But I ask this: if he did not mean to condemn the methods followed in negotiating this contract, what was his purpose in giving what I have called these vignettes? What was his purpose in putting those in the book? If it was not done in order that we

Bren Gun-Mr. Manion
might draw an inference, then the only conclusion I could arrive at would be that it was a lot of padding. I know Mr. Justice Davis slightly, more by reputation than personally, and I know that he would not put mere padding in this blue book. It is a complete condemnation of the department, even at page 51, the same page from which the Prime Minister quoted as to the exoneration so far as anything in the way of corruption was concerned. That is where Mr. Justice Davis recommends a defence purchasing board. I should like to read a few sentences, to give the gist of what he recommends at page 51:
_ What is plain to me at the end of this long inquiry is this: that if the policy of private manufacture of war munitions and armaments is to be continued in this country-
Then I jump a few lines.
-the purchase or production of such munitions or armaments should be put into the hands of an expert advisory group of competent business men-a capable and experienced manufacturer, a commercial lawyer who has had a wide practice in dealing with large commercial contracts, a representative of labour and say a chartered accountant who has had experience in the examination of substantial business transactions.
Then he adds:
These persons should constitute a board (which might be known as the "defence purchasing board") and be made directly accountable to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Finance.

this defence purchasing board should be put under the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance, and not under the Minister of National Defence. We will draw our own conclusions, as my hon. friends have a perfect right to draw theirs. I have drawn mine, and it is very clear to me what that means. To me it is a complete condemnation of the Bren gun contract and the methods by which it was negotiated. And I say, sir, that the whole report, with which I shall deal briefly, is a devastating condemnation of the department and of the government of which it forms a part.
Perhaps first I should give a few dates with which we will be dealing as we go along. The contract was made on March 31, 1938. It was announced in the press on May 5, a little more than a month later, and was tabled in parliament on June 29, nearly two months later. Though parliament was sitting all that time, it was not tabled until two days before parliament prorogued. I do not know whether any explanation has been made as to why it was not tabled long before the end of June. I ask myself-and I am not doing this in order to be unfair-whether it was because it was not considered desirable to table the contract until just before the house prorogued. That is a question one naturally asks; the minister will be able to answer it. I do not know the reason; I am asking the question. The article in Maclean's magazine, by Colonel George A. Drew, was published on September 1, 1938. These are four dates that it is well to keep in mind. It is now five months since the article was published, but until the Prime Minister spoke the other day he had made no pronouncement in regard to this matter. It is true that he appointed this royal commission, but what I find a little queer about the royal commission-or perhaps the word "queer" is not right; what I find a little strange about the royal commission is that although the commissioner was instructed to give his opinions, he was urged by all counsel, including government counsel, that he must not do so, that the only thing he should do was to set forth the facts. I should like to read what I think the Prime Minister read the other day, from page 4 of the report, where Mr. Justice Davis said:
The said commission required and directed your commissioner-

-to report as speedily as possible to our governor in council the result of his investigation together with the evidence taken before him and any opinion he may see fit to express thereon.
That is wide open; I agree that nothing could be more open. But, sir, if you turn to

He might easily overlook at a time like that a newspaper statement. Mr. Ralston is a busy man. At all events it was without effect

Even if he were instructed respecting freedom of opinion which Mr. Justice Davis was given, he paid no attention to it, and like the other counsel, did all he could- and I am making no reflection upon them-to stop Mr. Justice Davis from giving the opinions which the judge obviously wished to give. So that Mr. Justice Davis had to give them by inference, by little pictures and extracts from the evidence from which we could draw our own conclusions. In other words, what I find myself asking is this: Was Mr. Justice Davis instructed by letter to do one thing, and then was the whole investigation so hedged around by legal difficulties that Mr. Justice Davis could not make a proper investigation and a proper report?

In other words I find myself asking, was the whole investigation turned into a farce, in this way: that Mr. Justice Davis apparently desired to give opinions but was influenced so strongly by the views I have quoted, including the views of
Bren Gun-Mr. Manion

government counsel, that he did not, presumably, dare to do so? What was the attitude of the Department of Justice in the conflict between the argument of counsel and the order in council? The Prime Minister knows far better than I do that an order in council authorizing a legal investigation by a royal commissioner selected from the bench would probably be drawn up by the Department of Justice. I find myself wondering whether the Department of Justice made it clear to the government that, despite the letter of the Prime Minister to Mr. Justice Davis, this investigation would be hedged around by legal technicalities to such an extent that Mr. Justice Davis could not give what he thought was a just opinion. However, I am going to proceed with the case.
Here is what we find in the report. First, there was no competition. The matter was limited entirely to one man, Major Hahn, D.S.O., M.C. Without doubt this man had a splendid war record and there is nothing against him personally so far as I know. But the fact that a man has a splendid war record does not necessarily mean that he is capable of manufacturing Bren guns. I suppose there are at least thirty or thirty-five members in this house who are returned men, many of them with records just as good as Major Halm, but I should not like to ask them to manufacture Bren guns. There was no competition of any kind. That is one of the strange things about this whole matter.
The only business experience that Major Hahn had, so far as the record shows, was in connection with one venture-and may I say that I did not attempt to plough through four or five thousand pages of evidence, therefore I am confining myself to what Mr. Justice Davis says in his report. Major Hahn went into radio manufacturing. It is claimed that it was radio assembling, but it does not matter; he was selling radios as a manufacturer, if you will. Later on he went into the business of manufacturing other electrical appliances, such as washing machines. He continued in this business for about ten years. When the crash came in 1929 and 1930 the company began to get into financial difficulties, and it was finally necessary to sell out to the Rogers Majestic Company. The sale was handled in such a way in 1934 that the creditors of the company received only twenty cents on the dollar. This was the company of which Major Hahn was the head. Perhaps there is no disgrace in that; people in many walks of life have had to do the same thing, but neither is it a recommendation sufficient to make Major Hahn the only business man in this country who should be chosen to

manufacture Bren guns. On page 8 of the report it is stated distinctly that he was the only man who was given an opportunity I quote from the top of page 8:
Notwithstanding that the contract involves the expenditure of several millions of dollars by the Canadian government, no industrial producer (other than Major Hahn) was consulted by the Department of National Defence as to the proposed manufacture of Bren guns for the Canadian government or invited to give competitive bids or terms of manufacture. Nor did anyone so far as the evidence shows, ever visit any industrial plant (except Inglis) to consider the possibility of production of Bren guns in Canada. Mr. Hellmuth put certain questions to the minister iD this connection to which, with the answers, I now refer:-
Q. You did not give anybody else a chance?
A. Nobody asked for it.
Q. Mr. Minister, w'hat I want to get you to answer is this: You never did attempt in any method or any way to see what any one of these dozen or more well known companies, with skilled labour, skilled mechanics, who had been w-orking in precision steel-well, let us take the automobile industry which makes the very closest parts and closest tolerances-no effort %vas made of any kind to see what they could do?
A. The answer is "no." I do not think it was practicable.
That evidence proves that only one was given this opportunity. There was nobody else in competition with him.
Finally an order for 7,000 Bren guns was given on a cost plus basis. Major Hahn had a plant, the old Inglis boiler plant, which was reported as being capable of making boilers and certain other types of heavy machinery such as turbines. Certainly the plant at that time was not capable of manufacturing munitions, shells, Bren guns or anything else of the kind. It had been closed for two or three years. Many other plants in Canada were operating on precision steel, as they term it-automobile plants for instance. Mention was made of the Steel Company of Canada, the Dominion Bridge Company, and a number of others, any one of which would have been better able than the plant which Major Hahn had, to do such fine work as the making of machine guns.
On top of that evidence there is the strange circumstance that the minister himself in giving evidence-and I believe the Prime Minister said the same in the House of Commons last year-took the attitude that the manufacture of munitions of this kind should be done under government ownership. I shall quote from pages 10 and 11 of the report.

I agree with that. I join with the right hon. gentleman on that question. I have taken the same attitude right along. I took it in Geneva, in 1934, as the head of the Canadian delegation to the League of Nations. Many other public men have taken the same attitude, so there is nothing new in that. I am merely pointing out that the Prime Minister took exactly the same position.
The next point to which I want to draw attention-it is a little out of chronological order-is a letter written by Mr. Plaxton, the hon. member for Trinity, to the Prime Minister, dated August 24, 1936, and it appears on page 17 of the report. I quote from the report:
Mr. Plaxton wrote a letter to the Prime Minister (Exhibit 336) on August 24, 1936. This letter was written by Mr. Plaxton while he was in Ottawa, and at the request of his brother, Mr. Herbert Plaxton, who had telephoned him from Toronto. The letter reads as follows:

"A group of friends of mine in Toronto are equipped fully to manufacture munitions."
I emphasize that-"equipped fully."
Their plant is located in my constituency.
We know very well that that statement was just not true, to put it in the simplest language. They were not equipped fully. They had this more or less broken down Inglis Company plant. That letter was deceiving the Prime Minister; whether intentionally or not, I am not discussing. I am simply stating that the letter was deceiving the Prime Minister. The letter also says, "A group of friends." Now the group was Major Hahn, a brother, or two brothers, of the member himself, and the firm of Cameron, Pointon and Merritt, in Toronto. That was the group.
I turn to the next page, and I quote the evidence given by Mr. Plaxton, the member for Trinity. This is from page 18 of the report:
Mr. Plaxton was asked during his evidence who were the "group of friends" of his in Toronto who were fully equipped to. manufacture munitions at the time he wrote the Prime Minister on August 24, 1936, and his answer was:
"A. I was speaking as of that date of Major Hahn, Cameron, Pointon and Merritt, and Mr. Herbert Plaxton.
Q. And Mr. Gordon Plaxton?-A. No, not at that time.
Q. They were the group of friends who were fully equipped to manufacture munitions?- A. Yes.
Q. Where?-A. At the Inglis plant.
Q. How did you know that?-A. Well, I did not. I assumed as of that date that, speaking from memory, the deal was virtually concluded or had been-I was not definite as to any date."
That is the answer of the hon. member for Trinity.
The Prime Minister replied to the letter of the hon. member (Mr. Plaxton) on September 12, 1936, about three weeks after he had received it. The Prime Minister said in his letter to Mr. Plaxton-I hope the house will forgive me for saying "Mr. Plaxton" instead of the hon. member for Trinity, but it makes the record more clear-Mr. Plaxton having asked him if Canadians had the right to get contracts from the British government:
It would be necessary-

They send the gun to Toronto for him to examine. On October 19, 1936, ten days later, Major Hahn came again to Ottawa. He was staying at the Chateau Laurier. I will deal with that point right now, although it means I shall have to anticipate somewhat. When Major Hahn and Mr. Plaxton got over to London they called on Mr. Vincent Massey. He is a very capable civil servant, and he showed intelligence in this matter. He did not, on the word of the Department of National Defence alone, want to push Major Hahn along too fast. Mr. Massey had been asked to get appointments with the British War Office for Major Hahn, so Mr. Massey cabled to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in Ottawa this message, which appears on page 24 of the report:
Secret 396. Have received to-day following request in a wireless message direct from National Defence, Begins:
"Please request Major Hahn now in England to communicate with me through your office in cypher his impression as to possibility of producing Bren gun in Canada. This is urgent and ask him to give details such as time required for delivery and estimated cost. Ends."
In order to obtain information desired. War Office must be requested to give Major Hahn, as representative of the Canadian government, access to information of a secret nature which normally is not given to other than government officials.
Major Hahn also informs me that Minister of National Defence has requested him to obtain, if time permits, all available information regarding manufacture of tanks and shells which would also necessitate similar requests from the War Office.
Before making any application to war office, would appreciate instructions. Would be grateful for such instructions by to-morrow if possible.
This message was transmitted by External Affairs to the Department of National Defence, and, in reply, is a cable (exhibit 99), on November 10, from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the High Commissioner in London.
That is the Prime Minister.

I do not blame him much if he has read the report, but since he takes that attitude I emphasize it, because it has gone all over the country that apparently it was the Minister of National Defence who made Major Hahn the representative of the government. Now, I have gone ahead of my story, because I did not intend to deal just here with that aspect of the matter.

Surely a letter of recommendation of that kind should be regarded as more sacred than to be given to someone whom the minister did not even remember. He said he did not know Major Hahn last year. Last year, in the House of Commons, he said he did not know him until after the contract was signed, and yet in 1936 he gave this gentleman a letter of recommendation. On page 19, the report states:
_ Following upon the interview with the Minister on October 19, 1936, and without waiting for the report of the inspector who had been asked by the department on October 10 to inspect the Inglis plant in Toronto there was sent by the Deputy Minister of National Defence to the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, on October 20, 1936, the following letter (exhibit 74), suggesting, in view' of Major Hahn's early departure for England, the desirability of communicating with the high commissioner as soon as possible.
The letter says in part:
Major J. E. Hahn, D.S.O., M.C., a former officer of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and representing a reliable group which controls certain manufacturing plants-
Note the plural.
-capable of manufacturing armament and munitions located in a large industrial centre where the labour and material factor is stable and favourable, has been in communication with the department.
71492-42J
And Mr. Justice Davis, on page 21, draw's attention to this. He says:
It is to be observed that the letter states that Major Hahn represents a reliable group which controls certain manufacturing plants capable of manufacturing armament and munitions located in a large industrial centre where the labour and material factor is stable and favourable.
Then the deputy minister appeared before the commission. He was asked:
Do you mean to say now-
That is, two years later.
-that when you wrote that letter on October 20 you did not know the names of the individuals who made up that group?-A. No, I did not, but I did know that Major Hahn was a leading figure in the whole thing, he had a controlling interest and he had grouped w'ith him worth-while people, which is the natural thing.
Q. How did you know that-A. I was told it.
Q. By w'hom?-By himself and by Mr. Plax-ton.
Q. Anybody else?

A. No.
And further:
Q. You did not know on October 20

That is 1936:
-who Major Hahn's associates were? Do you know now who Major Hahn's associates were, in the enterprise?-A. I am not certain that I do know who they are now, no.
This was two years later, last October. A little lower down the commissioner reports:
The deputy minister had asked Major Hahn on his first visit on October 9, 1936, that the Inglis plant be inspected and that was done by the resident inspector (aircraft inspection detachment) at Toronto, whose report is dated October 21, 1936.
That is an interesting date. He gave the letter to the under-secretary of state on October 20, 1936, and he did not get the report on the plant "until the following day, yet he says he not only had the plant but he had plants. And the report said in part:
This plant is primarily equipped for the manufacture of boilers, turbines and the working of heavy plate generally. All equipment is in reasonably good condition, considering the length of time it has been in use.
The machinery at present in this factory with few exceptions, is unsuited for the manufacture of aircraft, but it might be used for the manufacture of tanks or shells.

It was October 26, 1936, that Major Hahn, Mr. Gordon Plaxton and Mr. Hugh Plaxton left for England.

Major Hahn and Mr. Hugh Plaxton called upon Mr. Massey, the High Commissioner, upon their arrival in London and gave to him the

The minister and the deputy minister were examined as to their knowledge of the "reliable group which controls certain manufacturing plants." The letter of October 20, 1936 (exhibit 74) having been read in full to the minister, Mr. Hellmuth asked him:
Q. Did you know at that time who Major Hahn's associates were?

A little further down the question is put to the minister by Mr. Hellmuth:
Q. I would like to have that question answered, with all due deference. I would like to know whether you knew whether Major Hahn had or controlled any plant or plants.
A. Not to my own knowledge-certainly not.

A. Not to my knowledge, no.

A. That is quite correct. [DOT]

steel?
A. No, not to my own knowledge.

And on the next page:
Q. So that you are still-I do not wish to say this at all offensively-you are still in the dark as to who these associates are and the group behind him?
A. I think we all are.
The deputy minister swore that he too did not know who were the "reliable group" which controlled certain manufacturing plants.

Bren Gun-Mr. Manion
Now, that is an interesting picture. They recommend Major Hahn very enthusiastically, send him across there to get information from the British government, make him a representative of the Canadian government, yet two years later none of them appears to know who Major Hahn's associates were, who this " reliable group " were, where these plants (plural) were-in fact there were not any " plants," there was one plant in Toronto. In addition there was pressure put on the British government in regard to this. For instance at page 44 the commissioner said:
That the Canadian department pressed the war office in the matter up to at least November, 1937, is frankly admitted. The minister stated the situation generally in these words in his evidence:
... it was a sustained endeavour to press the British authorities for a decision as to whether they would produce in Canada or not.
How do these words fit in with what I quoted the Prime Minister as saying, that Major Hahn must get the contract himself without the Canadian government intervening? And further down:
As early as December 24, 1936, the minister had revised and approved a letter (exhibit 107) to External Affairs requesting that a cable be sent to the government of the United Kingdom. . . containing these words:
Canada is prepared to proceed if war office can place initial order for not less than 5,000 Bren guns.
Then on April 20, 1937, the deputy minister wrote Doctor Skelton, the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, as follows:
On discussing the matter with my minister this morning he requested that I explain the great importance and urgency of this problem and to request that immediate action be taken to assist Major Hahn who evidently intends to remain in London for a few more days.

That is a question upon which the government and parliament, in the light of the evidence brought before the commission, must pass.

As one of the members of this house I would certainly say that "no" is the answer to that question.
The government and parliament have all the facts. I have given from this fifty-two page report what I think are the outstanding facts, and therefore I say, why should a committee be appointed? There has been already great expense. It would mean that the evidence would be repeated, and without any doubt it would end-I say this not disrespectfully-in the old way that all these committees do end, that is in a political whitewash.
What conclusion can we come to after all this evidence? If Mr. Justice Davis wishes to find only as the Prime Minister quoted the other day from page 51, that there was no evidence of corruption, why did he include all these pen pictures of startling incidents shown in the evidence? It does not require much imagination to answer that question. The reason was that he considered the whole

thing was irregular. I have touched on some of these points; but almost every page, nearly every paragraph in the report, criticizes the whole deal. It receives the greatest condemnation, as I have already mentioned, in the suggested appointment of a defence purchasing board, which by the way was recommended as far back as November 1936 by the conference of defence associations of Canada and was recommended in February 1938 by the artillery association; but nothing has been done until now.
My submission is that the whole report is one of political patronage in its worst form, favouritism to one man, Major Hahn; injustice to other industrialists far more capable and fully equipped-which Major Hahn was not; deception of the Prime Minister in the letter from the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton); of the interdepartmental committee by the various statements made to it by officers in authority; of the British government; and of the people of Canada. Has the Prime Minister-I ask this in all sincerity-read the report completely? Frankly it seems to me impossible that he could have read the report and not have condemned the whole deal.
Has he followed public opinion in the press? Take for example the two papers in this city, the Journal and the Citizen; the two newspapers in Winnipeg, the Free Press and the Tribune; the Toronto Telegram, the Financial Post and Saturday Night. These, to name only a few, as well as other papers across the country, have condemned the deal. In the debate on the address, I twitted the Prime Minister upon being too much interested in external affairs to be really interested in or understand internal affairs and the needs of the people, and upon not having been within a thousand miles of his own constituency since the last election. In reply, he said:
The position of the leader of a government in Canada to-day is not unlike that of the captain of a ship when the ship is in a storm. The captain of the ship must not be spending his time wandering among the passengers on the decks; his place is at the helm.
Well, we have 11,000,000 passengers on the ship of state which the right hon. gentleman is controlling at the present time; over 800,000 are on relief and over 450,000 unemployed, and they are not in a very docile mood to put up with such matters as this Bren gun contract. Indeed the right hon. gentleman's metaphor was not a particularly happy one, because in a modern ship the captain does not stay at the helm; he has helmsmen to do that. He goes down among the passengers daily, inspecting the vessel, and what is more, he keeps his eye on the crew-a very important thing to do. I
think it about time that the captain of this ship of state took a look at his crew and at the passengers. Does the Prime Minister endorse these pernicious proceedings? I use the word "pernicious" advisedly because to me that is what they are. A man who at that time was not manufacturing anything, so far as I know? I am not taking any different attitude with regard to munitions from that which I have taken for years. At the League of Nations in 1934 I took the attitude on behalf of the dominion government that there should be nationalization of the manufacture of munitions. I think my right hon. friend has taken the same attitude on some occasions, and the Minister of National Defence has taken it on a number of occasions. A few months ago in London, speaking before the Kiwanis club, and again in Toronto before the Commercial Travellers' Association, I took the same attitude. I took the same attitude and put myself on record in my speech in the house at the opening of the session. I said that huge profits in munitions were repugnant to the people of this country. I said it was like taking blood money, that it was profiteering in patriotism. I went on to say that munitions for Canada should be manufactured without profit, that the manufacture of munitions for Great Britain should be so completely controlled that an absolutely fair deal would be given to the British government. I said that we should have the absolute confidence of the British government and that we must have a new deal in munitions.
This is not ordinary government business. No one can deny that this is a question of life and death, a question of peace and war; it is a question of the life of our boys. It is a question of the safety of this country, and perhaps it is more than that, it is a question of our freedom as a nation. Are we going to carry on as we have? Surely not. The Prime Minister has expressed high ideals on democracy and on social justice, and so do
I.	I say that if we are to preserve democracy, if we are to preserve our social system, these ideals will have to be lived up to better than they have been in the past. And this applies not only to my right hon. friend and his government, but to other governments as well.
The Prime Minister alone can clean this up, and he must clean it up. On this depends the faith of the people of Canada. On this depends national unity and understand-

Bren Gun-Procedure
ing. On this depends confidence in the parliament of Canada, indeed confidence in the whole British parliamentary system. People across the country are asking themselves if democracies are worth while, if they are comparable with dictatorships. We all know that our democracies have very serious defects. As I have said many times, if we do not cure these defects, then to my mind the end of democracy is in sight.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister can clean this up, and he can do it quickly. There is only one way in which he can do it, and that is by cancelling the Bren gun contract. There need be no injustice done to Major Hahn and the John Inglis Company in that action. Out of pocket expenses could be paid. The work that has been done need not be lost because the government can expropriate the plant. To my mind that is the only way in which the confidence of the people of this country in our democratic government can be restored. That being my opinion, I desire to move, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) that the motion be amended as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
" In view of the evidence produced before the royal commission the opinion of this house is that the agreement made between His Majesty the King, represented by the Hon. the Minister of National Defence, and John Inglis Company, Limited, for the manufacture of Bren machine guns, should be cancelled."

speechtext:
The
motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) is what is called a routine motion. It is a motion to refer a certain matter to a committee of this house. Under the rules of the house this motion is debated on routine proceedings, and not in the ordinary way as are other motions of *which notice is given by an hon. member.
The amendment which is proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) would have the effect of changing the motion before the house into one which could not be debated on routine proceedings. The motion of the hon. leader of the opposition asking that a certain step should be taken by the government is a motion that should be put under notices of motions, like all other resolutions proposed by members of the house, and I submit that it is out of order.
I wish to call the attention of your honour to citation 132, page 41 of Beauchesne, which describes what is a motion allowed on routine proceedings:
The motions allowed on routine proceedings are motions relating to the business of the house and for the discussion of reports from committees.
Obviously the motion before the house, if the amendment of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is accepted, is no longer a motion that comes under routine proceedings. I would also call the attention of your honour to citation 397 of Beauchesne:
An amendment must not raise any question which by the rules of the house, can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice.
The motion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, just like any similar motion proposed by a member of the house, could not be moved without notice, and the fact that he tries to substitute his motion for that of the hon. member for Vancouver North, which could properly and did properly come under the routine proceedings, does not give any validity to the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has confused two things. He has quoted a rule applicable to motions brought before the house under routine proceedings, and then applied it to a motion which is already properly before the house. The closing words of the right hon. gentleman that the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) was properly before the house marks the point of departure in this matter. To quote again the standing order which the right hon. gentleman cited, and referring to citation 130 we read:
The house may, by unanimous consent or upon motion after forty-eight hours' notice, make such alterations in the order of business as it deems advisable.
No one would contend for one moment that the motion we are discussing, the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North, is not properly before the house with the full consent of parliament, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself emphasized the other day that he was most anxious that the resolution should be considered; so I assume, your honour, that the motion is properly before the house.
The question now arises whether the motion which is offered as an amendment may be properly entertained by your honour. If we turn to standing order 48 and certain citations thereunder it will be found, I think, that this amendment is in order. Standing order 48 reads:
When a question is under debate no motion is received unless to amend it.
The motion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is to amend the original motion before the house.
Then citation 394 of Beauchesne states:
A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain
Bren Gun-Procedure

words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
The amendment follows the usual course followed in this and other parliaments, in that it leaves in the word "that," which has always been considered sufficient to maintain the status of the original motion, and then it proceeds to strike out all the words after "that" and to insert certain other words in place thereof.
Citation 395 of Beauchesne has this to say:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed.
No one, I think, will argue that this amendment is not relevant. The motion under discussion is to send a certain report to a committee of the house, and the amendment says that in view of all the evidence which has been produced-and this point was emphasized the other day by the Prime Minister-and in view of the consideration given to the evidence in the report of the commissioner, which the original motion suggests should be referred to a committee, it is unnecessary to refer such report to a committee because we have already sufficient evidence before us to warrant parliament in now indicating to the government that the contract be cancelled forthwith. So the amendment is strictly relevant to the question.
Citation 395 of Beauchesne continues:
Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
No one will deny that this amendment is both intelligible and consistent-possibly a little too intelligible.
Then citation 400:
An amendment that is merely an expanded negative cannot be proposed by the chair.
That, of course, is one of the most commonly accepted rules and is frequently applied. It cannot be argued that the amendment is a negative motion.

The object of an amendment may be to effect such an alteration in a question as will obtain the support of those who, without such alteration, must either vote against it or abstain from voting thereon, or to present to the house an alternative proposition either wholly or partially opposed to the original question.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to join with
the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) in protesting against what seemed to me to be an effort on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to curtail discussion. He quoted a rule which applied to a special committee and then said that in this instance the public accounts committee was in very much the same position as a special committee. If his reasoning applied, no hon. member who might express views in this house which prejudged a situation would be entitled to sit on that committee. If that rule of the Prime Minister were made general it would be quite impossible to carry on the business of almost any committee of this house. For example, there is no subject on which feeling runs higher than that with regard to privileges and elections. How could it be possible for the committee on privileges and elections to discuss matters in which a large number of members who were vitally interested had already expressed themselves? Take the committee on railways. In the past there has been a good deal of discussion with regard to branch lines and so on. Does the Prime Minister suggest that anyone particularly interested in the question would be debarred from taking part in the work of the railway committee? Almost everyone has some definite ideas with regard to railway amalgamation or even railway cooperation. Does that mean that no one with definite ideas should sit on the railway committee? And what about the committee on banking and commerce? I am quite sure that the whole Social Credit party would be absolutely debarred because they have definite ideas, as indeed many of us have. Unfortunately, perhaps most of the members of the house have definite ideas along orthodox lines especially when it comes to finance. Are they to be debarred from sitting on the banking and commerce committee on any special question that may come up there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend is misconstruing ivhat I said. He is speaking about the general powers of committees. My point was with respect to a specific matter, where anyone had committed himself in respect to a specific matter, and the question of his serving on a committee.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My point is that a great many specific matters come before the committees which I have just enumerated. If the general rule which the Prime Minister is seeking to lay down were adopted it would mean that the house could not carry on its ordinary committee work. The Prime Minister seeks to lead us to believe that the work of this committee will be judicial. I question that very much. The work of the committee, if this motion is carried, is to find out whether public money is being wisely expended, and if somebody's toes are stepped on in the course of finding that out, all the worse for that person. The committee is not in any sense a judicial committee.
I did not think the Prime Minister was well advised in what he stated with regard to the member of the supreme court who was appointed as commissioner. He urged that this judge would be completely disinterested because he had not been appointed under the Liberal administration but had been appointed by a Conservative government. It seems to me there is an inference there that the people generally would not have had the same confidence if the judge who was selected had been appointed by a Liberal administration, and I respectfully suggest that after that statement the Prime Minister will have to be careful in his future selections to see that any judge who is chosen for any such position is one who has not been appointed under a Liberal administration. Otherwise, the public will draw their own conclusions.
I am in favour of the reference of this whole matter to a committee, because so far it has been quite impossible for the house to secure full and accurate information. In view of the large sums involved in the contract, my point may seem to be unimportant; but I think, in harmony with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has said, it is essential to maintain confidence in the parliamentary system.
The situation which I wish to emphasize is very important, because it involves the rights and privileges of the house. I refer to the minister's answers to my questions last year. My colleague a few days ago, on the orders of the day, asked a question in order that there might be no misunderstanding as to the accuracy of the record. The minister gave no
Bren Gun-Mr. Woodsworth

satisfactory information; he simply reasserted that the statements were "honestly, honourably and truthfully made."
I submit that such vehement protestations do not inspire confidence but rather tend to create the suspicion, "methinks the lady doth protest too much." I cannot know what is in the minister's mind; I cannot say that I am very much interested in that. It may be that the minister is ignorant in this matter; it may be that he has been misinformed; but the fact is that the house is entitled to certain information and the house has not received that information. Indeed, it received what I regard as misleading information. The minister's original statement, with regard to the Bren gun, as found in Hansard of 1938 at pages 2912 and 2913 is very sketchy indeed. He asserts:
The Canadian government has let a contract for 7,000 Bren guns to a firm in Toronto, the John Inglis Company Limited, I believe it is.
That is very offhand. One might judge that the minister knew the situation in only the most casual way.
Then came rumours that there was something very strange about the Bren gun contracts. And I asked these questions, answered in the house on June 22:
1.	Was Major James Hahn appointed by the Canadian government to go to England in 1937 and 1938 to make a survey of munitions production for the purpose of advising the Canadian government?
2.	If so, were his expenses paid by the Canadian government?
3.	What were the terms of Major Hahn's employment ?
4.	At what date did Major Hahn cease to be employed by the Canadian government to advise on munitions and begin negotiating for production by him of Bren machine guns?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver):
1.	No.
2,	3 and 4. Answered by 1.
It seems to me that the minister hides behind technicalities. Apparently I should have included in my question the year 1936. In his evidence as reported at page 2356 the minister said:
The question refers only to 1937 and 1938 and in my judgment the question is absolutely properly replied to or answered.
Well, if that is the kind of answer we are to be given, in the future we shall always have to put in a great many dates or general statements, such as " in the year 1936, 1937, 1938 or 1939 or any other year." I suppose that is the only way to get a definite and reliable answer from the minister. Major Hahn was apparently a promoter, then a representative of the government in one particular, and again a probable contractor.

This house has a right to know about such an arrangement. That was the reason for my questions.
Let us look at this question of dates. On October 19, 1936, there was a letter of introduction from the minister to the high commissioner in London. On November 10, 1936, there was a cable from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the high commissioner asking the latter to arrange with the war office to supply information regarding the Bren gun to Hahn, " as representing the Canadian government in this particular." On December 5,
1936,	Hahn wrote a letter to the minister enclosing a voluminous report of his investigations. On December 7, Hahn was in conference with officers of the Department of National Defence. On December 29, 1936, Hahn submitted a written proposal. In May,
1937,	during the imperial conference the minister was informed by the deputy that Hahn was making progress with the war office. He therefore became, in the words of the minister, at least so far as they were concerned " a probable contractor." That was in May, 1937, according to the minister himself. Up to that time presumably Hahn was a representative of the Canadian government. And the minister goes on to say:
I asked the deputy minister myself immediately to obtain for me some details of his company and of his financial standing.
Incidentally may I note that it was not until May, 1937, when Hahn became "a probable contractor" that the minister sought to find out anything about the details of his company or his financial standing. But I go on with these dates: In June, 1937, Hahn and the deputy minister were in England together. They saw the officials of the war office together. Remember that the minister had stated it as his opinion that Hahn had ceased to be a representative of the government and became a prospective contractor on December 5. That is the date of the report to the department of his investigations in England. He adds, however-I quote the minister himself->
On December 5, I take it in my judgment. It is a matter of opinion and argument.
Despite the admission of the minister that the point is one to be argued, a matter of opinion, he comes out in this house with his categorical "No" with regard to the whole series of questions. The second question I asked was:
2. If so, were his expenses paid by the Canadian government?
The answer is:
Answered by 1.

Bren Gun-Mr. Woodsworth
Let me point out that in 1937 Hahn put in a bill for legal fees amounting to something like $6,500; yet according to the minister he was no longer a representative of the government but only a probable contractor. Also he put in a bill for $7,191.31 for travelling expenses to England in the middle of 1937.
I would ask the minister whether Mr. Hahn was then a representative or a potential contractor. My question covered that period. Curiously enough, on this particular trip Hahn was said to be on private business. During the discussions regarding his contract Major Hahn was in Ottawa from March 14 to 18, 1938, and later submitted his bill for $326.80. It is true there is no evidence that I can find as to whether or not these bills were paid, but that does not alter my argument.
There is still another item that is of general interest to the public of this country with regard to moneys to be paid by the government to the company. Turning to the agreement we find at page 5 that:
A sum not exceeding $20,000 in respect of actual cost of preliminary investigation, planning and engineering services carried out by the party of the second part prior to the execution of the agreement as evidenced by vouchers-
Let me emphasize that. This large amount of $20,000 was to be granted for services rendered prior to the execution of the agreement. Yet the whole transaction was brushed aside by the minister in his answers to my questions by that one word "No".
My question No. 3 related to the terms of Major Hahn's employment, and I submit that this was not covered by the answer to question No. 1; it was a wide-open question, a very important one. But all the minister does is to say "No." Yet a few minutes later on that self-same day the minister said emphatically with regard to this same Bren gun matter that there was not the slightest intention to misrepresent the situation. I read the minister's own words as reported at page 4120 of Hansard of 1938:
I want to assure my hon. friend that there was not the slightest intention to misrepresent the situation.
Again a little later:
There was not the slightest intention to suppress nor was there a suppression of any information, in the slightest degree.
The minister, I may say, succeeded admirably in doing what he says he had not the slightest intention of doing; he succeeded in misrepresenting the situation to this house and in suppressing information that was highly necessary if we were to make an intelligent decision on the question at issue.
This brings me to another point. During the discussion of the defence estimates Mr. Bennett had asked whether the order from the British war office had not been secured through the good offices of the Department of National Defence. The minister replied, as reported at page 3555 of Hansard of 1938:
No; as a matter of fact I think negotiations were carried on entirely by the company's representative in England for the last two years, since 1936.
A week later I followed this up by a question with regard to United Kingdom munitions, and was told that the Department of National Defence played no part, directly or indirectly, in those negotiations. Let me read the Hansard report in order that we may be quite sure:
I have seen the article referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and I wish to assure him at once that the Department of National Defence has played no part either directly or indirectly in these negotiations. With reference to any orders to be placed in Canada, we have no more information than is in possession of the hon. member who asked the question.

The minister concluded :
I think that that is as definite as I can make the statement.
And the minister still maintains that position.

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is true, as the minister says, that the contracts were signed separately. It may be true, as he asserts, that he has no knowledge of the signing of the contracts. In that regard he may be correct, but I ask the minister, whether as he affirmed the other day, he had been answering the questions " honestly, honourably and truthfully." I am afraid that the house will be inclined to ask how honestly, how honourably and how truthfully. The house itself, and the public, must be the judge of that. Consider his own statements. Let me read from Hansard for 1938 at page 4120. I questioned him:
I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence, as it is asked both in the despatch and in a long editorial in the Free Press of last Monday, how he reconciles this state of affairs with his statement across the floor of the house to me the other day when he said:
"With reference to any orders to be placed in Canada, we have no more information than is in possession of the hon. member who asked the question."
Apparently there has been a joint arrangement between the British authorities and the Canadian authorities, together with a loan
Bren Gun-Mr. Woodsworth

of certain machinery from Quebec. If that statement is correct, how does the minister reconcile this seemingly very careful arrangement, and the signing of the contract, with his statement to me that he knows nothing more about the matter than I do?
The minister replied:
If my hon. friend will look over the discussions which took place in committee of supply when my own estimates were under consideration, he will find that in response to the question of some hon. gentleman opposite, details were very carefully stated at that time. There was no cooperative contract-
I call the attention of the house to this:
There was no cooperative contract; the contract with the war office was signed by the Toronto firm entirely separately from the contract with the Canadian government; but, as the result of the two complementary contracts being signed, there will be a saving to this government of over one and a quarter million dollars.
Later on he did seem to give some indication that there had been negotiations, for he said:
I say now in regard to these contracts that there has never been a cooperative effort between the British war office and the government of Canada except in regard to the Bren gun-
That was the very item and the only item under discussion. That is a most peculiar statement, which really I fail to understand. As I said a moment ago, it may be true that the contracts were signed separately, but there is very full evidence on the record showing joint consultation, cooperation and pressure prior to the contract. Take the report of the commissioner, from which I read this extract from the evidence:
Under such an arrangement guns sold to the Canadian government would carry their proper pro rata preparation cost. There are other obvious details which can be dealt with once the general basis has been found acceptable.
That is on page 26. Then on page 27:
-for cooperating in the form of "educational orders."
Then Mr. Geoffrion said this:
These two contracts are so fearfully interwoven that you cannot touch one without touching the other.
That is on page 32. Again on page 43 there is another interesting extract:
Then on March 28 or 29 Colonel Orde went to Toronto to represent the department in settling the terms of the British contract so as to make it uniform, so far as possible, with the Canadian contract.
All I can say is that if the minister does not know about the contract he should have known something about it. I want to read that passage once again:
Then on March 28 or 29 Colonel Orde went to Toronto to represent the department in

settling the terms of the British contract so as to make it uniform, so far as possible, with the Canadian contract.
Yet the minister dares to assert even today, as I understood his interruptions, that he knew nothing about it, that he had no more information than I had. The deputy minister, in his letter to the high commissioner's office on May 20 said in part:
For the reasons which I have outlined, the department ventures to suggest that it would be preferable to have the war office contract conform in detail with the one which the department has executed, but of course this is a matter for the war office to determine, and it is understood that the contractor will accept any changes by way of clarification which are desired.
That is on page 44.
That the Canadian department pressed the war office in the matter up to at least November of 1937 is frankly admitted. The minister himself stated the situation generally in giving his evidence, in these words:

it was a sustained endeavour to press the British authorities for a decision as to whether they would produce in Canada or not. That is the tenor of all the correspondence for nine or ten months in 1937-a sustained endeavour to obtain a decision from the war office as to whether or not they would place an order for Bren guns in the Dominion of Canada. That was carried on until November of 1937, I think.
Then the commissioner states:
That pressure from Canada upon the war office during the period was continuous is in my view the proper inference from the facts directly proved in evidence.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I confess myself to be utterly nonplussed. Whatever his motives may have been or whatever his capability may be, the minister did not give the house satisfactory information and, further, information to which the house was clearly entitled. All I can say is that the situation is a serious one. If the house loses confidence in the statements of the minister in the Bren gun affair, how can we have confidence in his statements when his estimates again come up for discussion in this house? It is especially serious when the minister is so largely responsible for the greatly increased estimates for national defence which are being presented to the house this year. I would urge that it is not merely the minister who is concerned in this matter; if the government maintains present arrangements, it must accept a very, very serious responsibility.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are reserving decision on the validity of the amendment which has been moved by my leader, (Mr. Manion) I shall not deal with that as I had intended to, but will refer to the motion itself, the motion of

Bren Gun-Mr. Stirling
the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), that the contract and the commissioner's report should be referred to the committee on public accounts.
On the last occasion that this matter was before this house, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) read from the report the reasons why the government had created a royal commission, and he read also the terms of reference which had been given to that commission-terms of reference so wide, I think, as to satisfy the general public of Canada that the investigation which was about to take place would be wide and general and that the report which would follow it would give the views and the opinion of the commissioner on the facts collected.
The Prime Minister went further than that, and explained his reasons for selecting the commissioner. He read a copy of the letter in which he expressed his appreciation that the particular commissioner had accepted the task, and he also read a statement which had appeared in the press at the time of the institution of the commission in which the view was expressed that the government would be ready to enlarge the scope of the inquiry if in the opinion of the commissioner that was necessary.
After thirty-five meetings of the commission, when all the evidence which appeared to be forthcoming had been laid before the commission, counsel one after another, began to make representations to the commissioner giving him advice as to what his report must not contain. My leader has referred to them, but I wish to emphasize one or two points which they raised.
First, counsel representing the John Inglis Company drew attention to the fact that the commissioner must suppress the word "misconduct"; he must go even further than that; he must see to it that he did not imply misconduct so far as that counsel's clients were concerned. He said-I am referring to page 32 of the report:
You are limited in your power to find facts, but your inability to find facts against us.
Then he made the reference to the fact that the British contract was outside the commissioner's jurisdiction.
Counsel who was affiliated with him in the representation of the John Inglis Company supported the views of the first counsel and also emphasized the fact that nothing outside the collection of facts should be contained in the commissioner's report.
Then, counsel for Plaxton and Company and the stockbrokers of Toronto, goes so far as to say that the commissioner would be forbidden to make a report against this counsel's clients. While this counsel had begun to address the commissioner, the commissioner asked the counsel for the government if he would be prepared to express an opinion with regard to limitations which might be put upon his, the commissioner's, words and the following day that counsel did express his opinion. It will be found at the top of page 34, and it is very much to the same effect as that of the other counsel. It is not very clear to follow, but he does make the point:
While government counsel said that there was no desire on their part "to whittle down your jurisdiction; nor is there any power or authority to extend it.
I suggest that with these views coming at the end of thirty-five days of inquiry, it was scarcely likely that the commissioner, at that late date, would turn to the government for an extension of powers to enable him to give the type of report that I for one, as a member of the general public of Canada, would have expected that commissioner to give. The commissioner does restrict himself; he restricts himself to the extent of saying this:
Having fully weighed the objection advanced on this ground

That is the charges of misconduct.
-as well as the weighty consideration brought to my attention by counsel that the rights of the individuals interested in the contract might become the subject of legal controversy elsewhere, I have come to the conclusion that it is inexpedient to comment upon the evidence in respect of its bearing on the conduct of the individuals concerned.
The facts are all in evidence; and as said by government counsel in opening their argument
So far as the facts are concerned, there are very few which are even in dispute.
I cannot recall myself at the moment any fact to which direct proof was adduced that is in dispute. It will be for those charged with the responsibility of dealing with the facts, i.e., the government and parliament, to examine and study them and to take such action, if any, thereon as they may see fit.
I turn to page 50 and quote again the words of the commissioner:
What is obvious, of course, is this: that if the government has an article to be manufactured for which by its very nature it is not practicable to call for tenders and the policy of private manufacturer is to be adopted, then at once the heaviest sort of responsibility falls upon those charged with the duty of selecting the individual, firm or corporation to manufacture the article. The question is: Were proper and sufficient steps taken in this case to discharge that responsibility? Upon the whole evidence, that is a question for the government and parliament to pass upon.
That is the gist of the report of the commissioner. And the Prime Minister's wish is that this matter should be referred to the
Bren Gun-Mr. Stirling

public accounts committee. Rarely if ever in my fourteen years in this house has the public accounts committee met; but from a reading of Canadian political history in years before that I find that the public accounts committee has been the ground for the fiercest sort of political battle. The government of the day would have the majority representation on that committee-

-and the object of the government supporters on that committee would be to ensure as far as they could, by such means as were at their disposal, that criticism of the government of the day should not be contained in the report of that committee. The public accounts committee as set up is composed of thirty-six Liberals, eight Conservatives, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) and two of his associates, and three members of the social credit group. I cannot bring myself to believe that any further light will be allowed to be shed on this matter by government supporters if it is sunk in the public accounts committee. If the commissioner had had suggested to him by government counsel that he should not report thus, and he had to content himself with collecting facts and emphasizing them as he did most notably, I do not consider that there will be any probability that we shall be allowed to be told in the public accounts committee some of the things which will have to be told before the public of Canada can really understand this matter.
Every time I read or think of this matter I ask myself: Why was Major Hahn selected? How did he become the favourite of the government? When the minister's estimates were before the house last session, reference was made by myself to an investigation which was being carried on as to the potentialities of Canadian industry as far as the manufacture of munitions, guns and other armaments was concerned. At that time I asked him if the Bren gun contract was a case in point. I asked if the Bren gun contract was one of the pieces of work undertaken as a result of the findings of the committee of inquiry into industrial possibilities, and the minister answered that it was.
Shortly after the minister took charge of the department he started this inquiry. I do not know the number of firms which had been investigated at the time Major Hahn was introduced to him, but by the time the contract was signed between seven and eight hundred firms had been investigated as to their potentialities. I am of opinion that at the time the introduction took place the minister

must have been in possession of facts which would have led him to believe that Major Hahn was far from being the only possible contractor for this purpose. But he was selected and he proceeded to England. Accompanying him was a letter of introduction which the minister had written and which he tells us was written on behalf of a man whom he did not know. It was a letter of introduction which was to take Major Hahn as far as the high commissioner's office in London. About the same time as that interview the deputy minister of national defence wrote a letter to which reference has been made already. This letter, to be found on page 20 of the report, was addressed to the undersecretary of state for external affairs. Its object was to enable the under-secretary of state for external affairs to prepare the high commissioner for the coming of Major Hahn so that the doors of the war office might be opened to him. The question of the inaccuracy and misleading nature of that letter has been drawn already to the attention of hon. members and I shall not stress this any further.
It should be remembered that at this time the deputy minister of national defence, upon whom the minister so properly relied and for whose work the minister properly takes full responsibility, was able to associate himself in this ordnance matter with the master general of the ordnance. The master general of the ordnance had been retired in 1934, I think it was, and given the customary twelve months' leave of absence. The Liberal victory occurred in 1935, and just before his year of leave had expired the position of master general of ordnance which had been abolished was recreated and this general officer was made master general of the ordnance. The deputy minister could scarcely be expected to carry all the details of Bren gun supplies in his head, but we must assume that the master general of the ordnance was in a position to keep the deputy minister straight on the matter. It is most unfortunate that the master general of the ordnance was not able to appear before the commissioner to give evidence of a technical nature which in the ordinary state of affairs he would certainly have done. Unfortunately his condition of health prevented his appearance. I draw no inference nor do I make any suggestion; I simply say it was most unfortunate under the circumstances that the evidence of the master general of the ordnance in connection with gun making was not available to the commissioner.
When Major Hahn reached London he found that the doors of the war office were not open and that he was unable to make the contracts he desired with the senior officers in

London having to do with matters of defence. The high commissioner did not see fit to give him an entree. Becoming disappointed with the delay, he telephoned long distance to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). The Minister of National Defence did not seem particularly ready to help him. So the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) sent two cables which are mentioned in the report. Immediately the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is the Prime Minister, sent a cable which has been referred to already and which indicated that he had taken Major Hahn under his wing to the extent of representing that he was Canada's representative in this particular Bren gun matter.
