speechtext:
Just before six o'clock the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was interjecting into my remarks his views with regard to the cable sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the high commissioner on November 10, and I think I understand now what the right hon. gentleman was referring to. He took it that I was connecting that cable with the one sent by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton). That was not at all my intention. I was dealing merely with the matter chronologically. Whereas these cables were of November 9, this was the tenth; and the Prime Minister is quite right in pointing out that his cable of November 10, sent from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was in reply to the cable of November 9, which he had received from the high commissioner.
Let us see how the Prime Minister's cable answered that of the high commissioner. The high commissioner, after referring to a wireless message from the Department of National Defence with regard to the possibility of producing the Bren gun in Canada, cabled the Secretary of State for External Affairs in order to obtain information:
	-
In order to obtain information desired war office must be requested to give Major Hahn, as representative of the Canadian government, access to information of a secret nature, which normally is not given to other than government officials.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Prime Minister, replying to this cable of November 9, acknowledges receipt of it; says that he had discussed the matter with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), and continues:
You might request war office to give Major Hahn, as representing the Canadian government in this particular-
And so on. I do not know in what way that will assist the Prime Minister in the position which he occupies, but it is quite correct that the one cable was in reply to the other.
I want to turn once more to the position occupied by the minister with regard to his choice of Major Hahn; for the first mysterious part of this whole mysterious question is: How and why was Major Hahn selected? I drew attention this afternoon to the fact that the minister, in the house in the session of last year, had replied to me that the Bren gun contract was one of the results of the work of investigation of the committee of inquiry into industrial possibilities, which certainly led me to suppose that as a result of the committee's inquiries Major Hahn had been discovered. I am afraid that after reading the contents of this report I cannot any longer hold that view.
I want now to draw attention to the position taken by the interdepartmental committee. The Prime Minister, just about the time he sent that cable to the high commissioner requesting that Major Hahn be selected as Canadian representative "in this particular", came to the conclusion that it was desirable to have a special committee set up which should inquire into the existing procedure for letting armament contracts. That was an important committee, the chairman of which was Doctor Skelton, and there were various most responsible members of the civil service thereon. It reported in a very few days that "the problem appears to be essentially an administrative one," and that seems to dismiss the special committee. In consequence of that report, what is known as the interdepartmental committee was created by the government by order in council on a certain date mentioned, and the Minister of National Defence was its chairman.
It is interesting to note that this interdepartmental committee did not hold its first sitting until just one year after the Prime Minister had made up his mind that a special committee was necessary, and at that first

Bren Gun-Mr. Stirling
sitting, to quote from the report in which the commissioner refers to the evidence of Mr. Elliott, the latter said:
The committee began to take an active part in the sense of asking questions, and getting to grips with the problem. In so doing the committee indicated that competitive bids should be one of the main considerations, and one of the first considerations. We pointed out that there was a number of very substantial subsisting companies in Canada that were manufacturing precision tools, and had had experience in what we thought was this line of work. We felt that they should be consulted and given an opportunity to submit competitive tenders. . . . The committee also thought there would be considerable time required for further consideration of the contract.
Mr. Elliott went on:
It early became clear to all members of the committee that there were two phases under consideration. One phase was that there might be competitive bidding . . . The second phase was the study of the terms of the contract in itself.
The committee therefore appointed a subcommittee of three, of whom only one was a member of the original committee, for consideration and study and report. Mr. Elliott said:
We recognized that we did not have the time to go into the necessary details to bring out the information in the form that we should have it. Therefore we simply asked this subcommittee to act as a sort of specific informer in connection with the terms of this contract and such other thoughts as might come about in the analysis of the contract for our guidance in considering this matter as a committee.
The subcommittee made its report a few days later, and that report contained in part the following:
Having in mind the main committee's suggestion that competitive bids be called for, the subcommittee, as an indication only of the names of concerns from whom competitive bids might be asked, mentioned-
The Steel Company of Canada
Dominion Bridge
Canadian Car and Foundry Company, Limited
Bertram Company
National Steel Company and possibly automobile manufacturers who undoubtedly have suitable plants and precision tools, together with such others as, in the opinion of the main committee, might be asked to tender.
And then the subcommittee proceeds to deal with the details of the contract.
The second meeting of the interdepartmental committee was held on January 24, 1938, and Mr. Elliott was asked:
Q. What was the main subject of discussion at the second meeting, Mr. Elliott?
A. Competitive bids and why the John Inglis Company should get this contract, the financial status of the company and a number of other things.
The committee wanted to get price comparisons from other competent companies. They felt the lack of them in considering this individual contract. They kept urging for some method of competitive bidding and comparative prices being entered upon.
Again I remind hon. members that the minister's investigating committee of inquiry had by that time unearthed a considerable number of firms in Canada capable of taking on this very work. But Major Hahn was the selection.
The deputy minister, as chairman of the meeting said he felt
that while competitive bids are always desirable, in this case there was a record of a substantial saving, a potential saving to the ' government, and that, together with the pressure from the war office for action, to get on with the job, we should enter into consideration of the terms of this contract with the Inglis Company.
And then Mr. Elliott refers to the fact that .because of his official connection with income tax affairs he was aware of certain difficulties which the old John Inglis Company had met with. Mr. Elliott continued:
The chairman indicated that he had an understanding-exactly how it was acquired I do not know-from England that they would not deal with any other firm.
Pressed as to exactly what was said, Mr. Elliott put it this way:
" I said as a statement of fact that the chairman stated to us that he believed, or he was of the opinion, whichever you wish to put it-he believed that England would not place the contract with any other company in Canada.
Mr. Elliott said that the suggestion was then made that a cable be sent to England to ascertain definitely England's position in respect of competitive bids.
The chairman pointed out that to ask such a question at this juncture might endanger the placing of the British order, and endanger thereby the loss which he obviously was anxious to save Canada in the cost of the machinery and equipment. . . The form of the cable was then drafted."
And we know the cable was amended with the subsequent approval of the committee, and was sent.
Then the deputy minister happened to meet Major Hahn in Ottawa. He had not been called before the committee, but at Major Hahn's suggestion the committee had been continued. Major Hahn unexpectedly goes to England, and is back on February 18, before the third meeting of the committee. That was February 25. Mr. Elliott said:
The committee then swung into the repetition of this statement, namely the fact that competitive tendering had not been entered into by three or four companies capable of manufacturing guns and that that was one of the main objections still tentatively retained by members of the committee.
An important matter then developed, so far as the committee was determined by the chairman indicating that responsibility for the way in
Bren Gun-Mr. Stirling

which this particular company had been selected necessarily rested with the Department of National Defence.
Mr. Elliott said that the chairman-the Deputy Minister of National Defence-pointed out that-*
his department had followed the practice of the British government where competition is not always obtainable, and they unhesitatingly go into non-competitive contracts in order to secure their requirements. In this particular case the British government had picked the firm to manufacture its guns.
By the Commissioner:
Q. Just a minute; the British government had done what?
A. Picked the firm.
Q. In this ease?
A. Yes.
Q. In this case the British government had done that?
A. Yes, that in this case the British government had picked the firm to manufacture guns, and that they had made the best possible deal with that particular firm.
Then Mr. Elliott described how that completely reorientated them in respect to the whole matter. The interdepartmental committee assumed that the Department of National Defence took at least that onus off its shoulders. I would remind hon. members that the minister in his evidence said that he made himself responsible for all the doings of his officials; that he accepted the reliable supervision of men in whom he had absolute confidence, and that he was leaning on the recollection that he knew that in the end the whole situation was to be thoroughly reviewed by the subcommittee of the interdepartmental committee. Yet the work of the interdepartmental committee at meeting after meeting was to the effect that they were not satisfied, and were not going to let the matter go because they were not satisfied. Once again the committee .wanted to cable to London; they wished the cable definitely to ask the war office, "Do you adhere to the view that you must deal with that selected contractor or not?" That cable was never sent.
The motion is to refer this matter to the committee on public accounts. I have already indicated that I would have absolutely no faith in that treatment of this matter. I wonder whether in this regard members of the government recollect, as I certainly believe they must, that the Prime Minister and his 179 followers in this house occupy those seats under the sufferance of 46 per cent of the electors who voted Liberal in 1935, and that 54 per cent of those who voted in 1935 voted against Liberal candidates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to be able to speak on the amendment to the motion which was  moved by my honoured leader (Mr. Manion). But as you, sir, have reserved your opinion on this matter, I am forced to speak to the motion itself, which is to refer the matter of the Bren gun contract to a standing committee of this house. I am sure that all hon. members have noted the almost acrobatic willingness of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) to have the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Mac-Neil) carried, and thus to have another extensive and expensive investigation conducted, which in the opinion of many of us would be a great redundance. Last autumn there was a most thorough investigation by a royal commission presided over by no less a gentleman than a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. The inquiry was characterized by the virtue of completeness, and that virtue is best expressed in the words of Mr. Justice Davis himself at the conclusion of the report, when he says: -
All the sittings of the commission were public and your commissioner was pleased to hear counsel characterize the inquiry, at its close, as "a most searching and thorough inquiry."
Mr. Justice Davis states at the commencement of his report on page 4:
Your commissioner has had the assistance of the Honourable J. L. Ralston, K.C., Mr. L. A. Forsyth, K.C., and Mr. Jacques Dumoulin, K.C., appointed by the government of Canada as government counsel and to assist the commission; Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C., and Mr. J.	C. McRuer, K.C., who appeared for John Inglis Company, Limited; Mr. I. F. Hellmuth,
K.	C., who appeared with Colonel Drew, representing both Colonel Drew and the Maclean Publishing Company Limited which published the article in Maclean's Magazine which gave rise to this inquiry; and Mr. II. F. Parkinson, K.C., who appeared for the legal firm of Messrs. Plaxton & Company and for Messrs. Cameron, Pointon & Merritt.
The commission opened on September 19, 1938. and concluded on Thursday, November 24, 1938. The taking of testimony and the argument of counsel occupied thirty-six days.
Then later:
Your commissioner is satisfied that all available documents in any way relevant and material to the subject matter of the inquiry were presented to the commission.
The evidence taken before your commissioner extended to 4,122 pages of stenographic notes besides the documentary evidence, which was filed in 388 exhibits, and the argument of counsel was extended in the stenographic notes from page 4123 to page 4711 inclusive, all of which is returned herewith.
It is obvious that in the opinion of the learned justice the whole matter of the Bren gun contract has already been thoroughly threshed out; that the evidence compiled, as well as the report of the royal commission itself, are available to this parliament, and

Bren Gun-Mr. Massey
that any further investigation is merely unnecessary repetition at the public expense. I absolutely agree with the commissioner that there is no need whatsoever for this matter to be referred to a committee of this house, standing or special; that the evidence at hand supplies all the information necessary to any action which this house wishes to take in this matter. Let it be further borne in mind that on page 35 of the report the commissioner states:
The facts are all in evidence; and as said by government counsel in opening their argument:
So far as the facts are concerned, there are very few which are even in dispute.
I cannot myself recall at the moment any fact to which direct proof was adduced that is in dispute. It will be for those charged with the responsibility of dealing with the facts, i.e., the government and parliament, to examine and study them and to take such action, if any, thereon as they may see fit.
Also on page 49 of the report:
The contract is not for a fixed sum: it is on a cost plus basis. It is admitted that we do not know how much the guns are going to cost. There are of course adequate powers of inspection, supervision and control vested in the department under the contract and with the estimates from Enfield of what the guns there are costing it should be possible to keep actual costs here well within bounds.
No substantial objection can be taken in my view to the provisions of the Canadian contract; though in the absence of any competitive bids or terms of manufacture I am unable to pass upon the substance as distinct from the form of the contract. It is important, of course, that the contract be a good and businesslike contract; but what is more important after all is whether the procedure adopted in making the contract was that best calculated to protect the public interest and to secure the confidence of the people of Canada that there would be no improper profiteering in the private manufacture of war armaments for the defence of the country.
That is a question upon which the government and parliament, in the light of the evidence brought before the commission, must pass.
It is obvious then and beyond argument that Mr. Justice Davis considers that parliament may act upon this matter with the information at hand and feel fully satisfied that they are possessed of all the important factors relative to this unfortunate situation.
A study of the evidence and the commissioner's report reveals facts which, with the procedure followed up to the time of the signing of the contract itself and the nature of the contract, fully justify the amendment to the motion which was introduced this afternoon and which is still before the house, to the effect that the contract signed between the Canadian government and John Inglis Company Limited should be forthwith cancelled.
Let it be borne in mind that the Bren machine gun is an instrument of war, invented in Czechoslovakia and further developed to conform to British conditions. The agreement between his majesty's governments in Great Britain and the dominions for the manufacture of this gun for his majesty's forces at home and abroad covered not only the gun itself but the tripod and the filling machine as accessories. One of the conditions of the agreement is cited by Mr. Justice Davis at page 5 of the report:
. . . such manufacture shall be in a factory operated by the government in question.
Also in a memorandum dated June 3, 1936, from the director of mechanization and artillery in the Canadian Department of National Defence to the master general of the ordnance, it is further stated:
The privilege of so doing (i.e., production in Canada) was vouchsafed to the Canadian government by the War Office when it acquired the rights of manufacture from the patentee, the only stipulation being that such production must take place in a government-owned factory.
That is also on page 5. The Minister of National Defence and his deputy have stated what they consider to be their reasons for departing from this procedure; but the two reasons given, first, the vast expense to the Canadian government for the erection of plants for the manufacture of this gun, and, second, that Major Hahn was the only gentleman with whom the British government would deal, have fallen down miserably and have been found to be hopelessly unfounded I Thus perforce we should return at once to the highly desirable position of manufacturing these guns free from private enterprise and the obvious feature of profit to individuals in the manufacture of arms. Later in the course of my remarks I plan to deal more fully with that point.
Now to return to the contract itself. In the article by Lieutenant-Colonel George A. Drew which appeared in Maclean's magazine in its issue of September 1, 1938, various statements were made in regard to the contract which were not contradicted or disproved in any shape or form by the prolixious evidence given by the various witnesses at the inquiry. Let me quote a paragraph or so, starting at page 2 of the article:
It is true that there is a provision in the Canadian and English contracts which appears to limit the profit to ten per cent with an over-all limitation of $457,000 for the 12,000 guns covered by the two contracts, but there is another provision which overcomes that limitation. Section 6A provides that when the company is in production a "standard cost" for each gun shall be agreed upon, based on the costs up to that time. If after that
Bren Gun-Mr. Massey

time costs are reduced below that standard cost, the company shall receive one-quarter of the difference, in addition to its other profits. As the costs during the experimental stages are bound to be higher than when normal production has been reached, it is clear that this is likely to add a very substantial figure to the profits.
Was that statement disproved? It was not. Then again:
Agreements providing for production on a "cost plus" basis are not at all unusual. But many of the items on which the ten per cent profit is allowed in this contract are extremely unusual. Profit is in no way limited to actual factory costs. For instance, the government pays the salaries of executive officers of the John Inglis Company Limited, although their activities are not confined to the manufacture of machine guns. It also pays travelling expenses, and under the contract Canada would pay two-thirds of the cost of travelling which might be necessary to England or Czechoslovakia, where the gun originates. Not only that, but both salaries and travelling expenses are paid by the government from the date of the contract whether any machine gun is ever delivered or not. It is doubtful if such a contract ever was signed in Canada before. But even that is not enough. The company receives from the government as part of its "cost plus" profit, ten per cent of the amount of these salaries and travelling expenses from the date of the signing of the contract.
Other unusual items to be paid by the government, and on which ten per cent profit is also to be paid, are legal fees; telephone, telegraph, and other office expenses; cost of light, heat and power; of all plant alterations {including even the cost of removal of any or all machinery which may ever be removed), and the cost of all tools, dies, jigs and gauges, whether bought from the company or manufactured by the company itself, if they are to be used in the production of Bren guns. Nothing is forgotten. The government even pays for all cartridges and explosives used in testing the guns before delivery. The government, or rather the Canadian public, pays everything, and then pays a profit as well to the company of ten per cent of the amount of these already remarkably generous payments.
The least that can be said is that the contract is extremely favourable to Major Hahn and his company. Even if the contract is * cancelled before the company gets into production, the company will receive $43,750.
If the contract is cancelled to-night, Major Hahn and his associates receive S43,750!
The reason for this generosity is not given. As the government pays all costs of installation of machinery, of the machinery itself, and even of its removal, as well as profits and salaries in the meantime, the public might be inclined to think that it had already done enough for Major Hahn and his company. But the contract says that there must be a substantial profit in any event.
Has any one statement of those I have just read been disproved?

I thank my hon. friend.
Perhaps my idea of this chamber and its functions is too altruistic and too pristine; but for the three sessions I have had the privilege of sitting in this chamber I have been under the impression that our deliberations should have been characterized by an effort, on the part of all of us who take part, at frankness and straightforwardness and that no attempt should be made by any hon. member, let alone a minister or the Prime Minister, to mislead the house; that questions asked in the public interest should be answered in the public interest; that inquiries of a minister should be answered accurately without any attempt to mislead.
I have always felt that, and have accepted the answers by the ministers to questions upon the order paper as being predicated upon that basis. It may be I have assumed that position because I am naive in this house, but I have at least that hope for our deliberations.
But, in the matter of the Bren gun there have been statements made and answers given to questions submitted by hon. members that have certainly misled the house. The Minister of National Defence states with some heat that his statements in answers to questions have been "honourably, honestly and truthfully" made. I want him to understand that I do not challenge that for a single moment; but I do say to him that, as one reviews his statements of last year in the light of the evidence submitted to the royal commission, it is obvious that either one of two things has happened:	First, that he has
been victimized by a lack of information- which is his own fault-or, second, that he
himself has been misled-which also is his own fault. So it is his own fault in either case.
Let me review the sequence of events in this house towards the end of last session relevant to this matter. In a copy of Hansard of June 22, 1938, on page 4118, I read:
Mr. Woodsworth:
1.	Was Major James Hahn appointed by the Canadian government to go to England in 1937 and 1938 to make a survey of munitions production for the purpose of advising the Canadian government ?
2.	If so, were his expenses paid by the Canadian government?
3.	What were the terms of Major Hahn's employment ?
4.	At what date did Major Hahn cease to be employed by the Canadian government to advise on munitions and begin negotiating for production by him of Bren machine guns?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver):
1.	No.
2,	3 and 4. Answered by 1.
I admit at once that the answers of the minister to the questions I have just read are accurate, but poisonously accurate. It is obvious that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was asking it' Major Hahn had been a representative of the Canadian government. That was the question. Unfortunately, however, he specified 1937 and 1938, so the minister answered No." Major Hahn was, however, until December 5, 1936, about three weeks before 1937, a representative of the Canadian government to the British war office. Thus I declare, that question 4 which I have just read, At what date did Major Hahn cease to be employed by the Canadian government to advise on muntions and begin negotiating for production by him of Bren machine guns?" is not answered by the "No" which is given in answer to the first question. Major Hahn visited England subsequently to December 5, 1936. I should like to ask the minister, had the British war office been informed that Major Hahn was no longer the representative of the Canadian government? Was official word sent from his department subsequently to December, 1936, to the British war office that Hahn had ceased to be the representative of the government?

speechtext:
Yes, I shall come to that. In the eyes of the British war office Major Hahn continued to be the representative of the Canadian government in all his trips to England. He was received accordingly and was treated as such. Therefore I say that the answers given to the questions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are grossly misleading and should at least have been qualified by a statement of the Minister of National Defence when submitting his answer of June 22, last.
The opinion I have just expressed is that of a new member of this house; and lest I be accused of presumption or lack of knowledge, let me read to the house an editorial appearing in a newspaper which I do not think any hon. member can question is virtually the organ of the Liberal party in the prairie provinces. Certainly the Winnipeg Free Press could never be accused of Conservative tendencies; it could never be accused of supporting the Conservative party; nor has it ever disclosed any such desire. I have in my hand an editorial taken from the Winnipeg Free Press of October 27, 1938, headed "Mr. Mackenzie's Evidence":
There will be no satisfaction and much regret over the remark made by the Hon. Ian Mackenzie, Minister of National Defence, during his evidence before the Bren gun inquiry, that he was satisfied the statements he made in the House of Commons were correct. The fact is that very essential information was withheld from the house, which rose without the faintest idea of the most important circumstances surrounding the letting of the contract to Major Hahn.
This was hardly the fault of the members of the house. Various men made strenuous efforts to get at these facts. They failed because Mr. Mackenzie eluded them by making replies which, though perhaps technically justified under the rules of the house, were not justified at all when the public interest is considered.
Later in the same editorial:
On the same day that he "answered" Mr. Woodsworth's question he told the House of Commons this:
"I want to assure my hon. friend that there was not the slightest intention to misrepresent the situation . . . There was not the slightest intention to suppress nor was there a suppression of any information in the slightest degree."
Twelve days later, on July 1, he went back over ground he had covered before, and recited

his explanation of how Major Hahn got the contract. This has already been quoted by the Free Press. It is worth repeating once more:
"Major Hahn went to England in 1936 and evidently made a favourable impression upon the British people. He also had access over there to the specifications of the Bren gun. I want to leave the idea with the committee that these are secret specifications and we had no control over them. It is quite possible they would not be available to any competitor of the firm that got the contract."
Consider these two statements were quoted, and consider the facts as' they have since been brought out. We have Mr. Mackenzie's assurance that nothing whatever has been suppressed. Then we have his statement about Major Hahn's stand-in in London and the drag he had with the war office. Is there anything here to suggest to anyone that Major Hahn got the inside track because he was put there officially by the defence department? Is there anything on the record of Hansard to show that Major Hahn was treated by the British war office just as one more Canadian promoter until cabled instructions were received to consider him an official representative?
The impression Mr. Mackenzie left on the house-and it is difficult to imagine that so practised a debater would leave an impression on his audience other than that he wanted to leave-was that, quite independently of the Canadian government, Major Hahn had made "a favourable impression upon the British people." We now know, of course, how that came about. Major Hahn "had access to the specifications for the Bren gun." How did he get them? We now know, though the House of Commons did not. "It is quite possible the specifications would not be available to any competitor." We should say not; not after all the Department of National Defence had done for Major Hahn! But did Mr. Mackenzie breathe a word of all this to the House of Commons? Not one word. Why?

know. I just want to have that on record. Then the minister goes on, as reported on the same page:

IMr. I. Mackenzie.]
There is the fact that on October 9, 1936, Major Hahn was introduced to the deputy minister of national defence; and even though the deputy minister knew nothing about Major Hahn except that he had been introduced to him by the hon. member for Trinity, a secret Bren gun was sent to Major Hahn in Toronto for dismantling and examination. A secret war piece which had been given into the custody of the Canadian Department of National Defence by the British war office was sent to an unknown in Toronto for dismantling and examination. Does the mblister deny that statement? Further evidence was brought forward to show that Major Hahn was introduced to the Minister of National Defence in his apartment in the Chateau Laurier on October 19, 1936. After five minutes the minister gave Major Hahn a letter which subsequent events proved served to pave the way for Major Hahn to become the accredited representative of the Canadian government to the British war office. He was accredited by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself. Let me read the letter, which appears on page 17 of the report. It is dated October 19, 1936, and is addressed to Dear Mr. Massey." May I say that is not the member for Greenwood; it is the high commissioner in London. The letter reads.
The bearer of this letter, Major J. E. Hahn, D S O M C., is in England to investigate the manufacture of all classes of motions and armaments. I am anxious that lie be afforded averv facility and access to enable him to ascertain and bring back complete manufactur ing data and costs governing manufacture of
How can it be said that in connection with so vitally important a matter as the manufacture of the Bren gun, such an all-embracing document can be given to a private citizen and yet the experience foe forgotten by the minister? The agility and facility of his brain have never been questioned in this house. The best thing that can be said is that here is a manifestation of the most extraordinary careless dealing and the most extraordinary disregard of public interest. Let me quote again from page 4524 of Hansard, the minister
speaking:
Major Hahn went to England in 1936 and evidently made a favourable impression upon the British people. He also had access over there to the specifications of the Bren gun. i want to leave the idea with the committee that these are secret specifications and we had tin control over them.
No control over them! Yet they were sent to an unknown in Toronto. I quote again.
It is quite possible they would not be available to any competitor of the firm which got the contract. I want to say this: Once we were informed by the war office of the attitude

Bren Gun-Mr. Massey
of the British government we went into figures with the Enfield factory in England which produces those guns at the rate of fifty a week-
Here again is an extraordinary statement, that Major Hahn went to England, saw the British war office, was admitted to the Enfield factory and given the specifications of the Bren gun. That is a statement of fact. But how did this happen, and why did this happen? Why was it Major Hahn? Because Major Hahn was the accredited representative of the Canadian government, accredited by the Prime Minister himself; and with him, and with him only, would the British government deal. The British government did not deal with Major Hahn because they liked him or thought him to be the proper man as a result of their own opinion. The British government dealt with Major Hahn because, I repeat, he was the accredited representative of the Canadian government, and had received the benediction of the Prime Minister in this matter.

What is back of this? Major Hahn arrived in England, accompanied by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) and his brother, Mr. Gordon Plaxton. Let it be said to the resounding credit of the high commissioner in London that he refused at first to accept Major Hahn or to pass him through to the British war office until he was satisfied that Major Hahn was properly credentialed, and a delay ensued during which the major became, in his own words, "very, very impatient." There were telephone calls and cables until at last a cable from the high commissioner in London was sent to the Secretary of State for External Affairs-in other words, the Prime Minister-and Mr. Massey was answered by the Prime Minister as follows:
Secret. Your cablegram 9th November 396. Have discussed matter with Minister ^of National Defence. You might request War Office to give Major Hahn, as representing Canadian government in this particular, any information which they consider desirable and necessary to enable National Defence to reach conclusion on possibility produce Bren gun in Canada. It is not desired to request furnishing of information on any article other than this gun.
Under such circumstances, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious, then, that Major Hahn was not accepted as the representative of the Canadian government when he first arrived in England; that later he was established as such by a cable in code from the Prime Minister; and it was then, and only then, that he was received by the British government and given secret information.
What is the significance of this? The significance is that upon this thin and slender thread, the all-embracing decision to depart from the policy of arms manufacture by the government to arms manufacture by private citizens for profit was arrived at by the Prime Minister, by the Minister of National Defence and by the Department of National Defence.
Let us now return to the evidence. The interdepartmental committee objected strenuously to going forward in this matter without competitive bids, but they were told by the deputy minister of national defence, who presided at the sittings of the interdepartmental committee, that the British government had picked the firm with which they were going to deal. The whole argument so far has revolved around the fact that this man got a contract from the Department of National Defence. The discussions which have taken place in connection with that contract were given rise to largely by an article which appeared in Maclean's magazine under date of September 1 last, which article by the way, Mr. Speaker, made no charges against anyone but did give expression to quite a number of insinuations which might be taken by the general public as indicating that there was something wrong, if no actual charges were made.
Very shortly after that article appeared, we had a Commission appointed by the government to inquire into the insinuations which had been made and into the contract which had been entered into. After many sittings of that commission had been held; after the commission had found it unnecessary to subpoena any witnesses in order to get them to appear before the commission because all witnesses came quietly of their own free will when called upon to do so; and after they had listened to the evidence from day to day, the commission itself decided that there were no charges and no findings to be made, against any individual, and that there were no charges and no findings to be made in opposition to the contract which had been entered into. So that we are in the position, after having read the article in Maclean's magazine and after having listened to the evidence before the commission, where no proven evidence has been brought forward against either the contract itself or any individual who was associated with that contract or with the government or with departments of the government in negotiating the contract.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) presents to the house a resolution which calls for the placing of this

Bren Gun-Mr. Gardiner
contract for further inquiry before a committee of the house. The government takes no exception to that motion. The government is quite prepared to have this contract inquired into to the heart's content of any member, of this house or of any person outside this house, whether such persons are interested in newspapers or are other private individuals in Canada.
Well, the opposition-that is, the official opposition-comes along with an amendment in these terms:
In view of the evidence produced before the royal commission, the opinion of this house is that the agreement made between His Majesty the King, represented by the hon. the Minister of National Defence, and John Inglis Company, Limited, for the manufacture of Bren machine guns, should be cancelled.
We have before us at the moment an amendment calling upon the house' to cancel the contract with regard to which even the article in Maclean's magazine has not made any particular charges; with regard to which those who appeared before the commission did not make any charges; with regard to which the commission itself did not make any charges. We are asked, rather than to send it for further inquiry' to a committee of this house, to cancel that contract forthwith. Well, if that does not raise some questioning in the minds of hon. members as to what all the noise is being made for with respect to the individual Major Hahn, then I cannot understand what would raise that sort of questioning in the mind of anyone.
We listened this afternoon to a good deal of discussion beginning with the address of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) with regard to this matter, and even yet I have to hear any condemnation of the contract itself from the individuals who have been addressing this house. They have insinuated certain things and drawn certain pictures, so to speak, using, in order to describe those pictures, certain terms which even members of this house do not understand. They have left inferences with regard to what the contract may have in it; but I repeat that no one has risen in his place and told us what the terms of the contract to which they take such serious exception are.
I wish to go ove'r some things that have happened in recent months in connection with matters of defence to see if I cannot reason out for my own instruction the position with respect to this contract. I wish to indicate the position I have taken in connection with this contract from the beginning and the position which I hope the house will take with regard to it. There has been a great deal of discussion respecting what has appeared in
Maclean's magazine, and the hon. member who has just taken his seat has quoted extensively from it. I shall not quote from it, but I wish to direct attention to the fact that at the end of that article there are some twenty questions stated in such a form as to leave the insinuation that something might be wrong in connection with the matters referred to in every one of those questions. In the centre of that group of questions, beginning with number three and extending to the end of question twelve-there is some reference to it in later questions also-there is a group of questions all of which refer to the activities of certain private individuals who had to do with the formation of a company in the city of Toronto which eventually got a contract for the manufacture of Bren guns. There has been a great deal of quoting of the report in order to try to indicate that certain statements made by the commissioner in his finding had to do with everything that is in this report. If hon. members will turn to page 30, they will find the following:
A large portion of the evidence-
Here let me point out that the part of the report which I am about to read is separated from what goes before by asterisks.
A large proportion of the evidence taken before the commission was in connection with the facts leading up to and the purchase of the assets of the old John Inglis Company by Major Hahn and his associates, the financial structure of the new company, the shareholdings of the new company, the consideration given for the allotment and issue of the shares of the new company, the incorporation and organization. . . .
And so on. Then at the bottom of the paragraph there is this reference:
Mr. Geoffrion, who appeared with Mr. McRuer for the John Inglis Company, stated that, for purposes of argument, Major Hahn and the John Inglis Company may be identical, because he was the spokesman of the company and the party in control. Mr. Geoffrion. relying upon sec. 13 of The Inquiries Act, R.S.C., 1927, eh. 99, argued that as no charges of misconduct had been laid or been formulated during the inquiry, no report against any person can be made by your commissioner.
Then later:
Mr. Geoffrion said:
No charges being laid, no report of misconduct or no report can be made against us, because there was no charge of misconduct, and no notice to us.
"Us" there refers to his clients; and as one reads through statement after statement by counsel who appeared before this commission, one finds that they are referring to private clients who retained them to appear before this particular commission. The finding is finally made by the commission that
Bren Gun-Mr. Gardiner

in relation to these matters having to do with the formation of a company in Toronto, and with the individuals who formed the company, he is not making any findings because no particular charges were made against these individuals.
It should be clear to any member of this house that there are many things which he and I might wish to criticize with regard to the formation of companies from one end of the country to the other, companies dealing with the manufacture of machinery of different kinds, companies for the purpose of carrying on financial operations, companies for the conduct of many affairs. I could make many criticisms to-night from the floor of this house with regard to the formation of many such companies, but such criticisms would not have anything to do with many of the activities carried on by these companies when once they are set up, unless we are prepared in this house and elsewhere to change the whole company law of the country and make it impossible for people to set up companies under the forms which were followed in this particular instance.
It was proper for the commissioner on that occasion to make that reference, but it was entirely improper for the leader of the opposition this afternoon to say to the members of this house, and through the house to the people of Canada, that these statements were made by counsel on behalf of their clients apparently for the purpose of frightening the commissioner. I can think of no more slighting statement that could have been made against the chairman of any commission that ever sat in this country than to suggest that any counsel appearing for anyone could frighten the commissioner when making a finding in connection with this or any other matter.

And I repeat that statement to my hon. friends in this house. If they think that you can go about this country giving out contracts to people before they have been given some training, in order to bring about the production of these different commodities, then they are going to find themselves in considerable difficulty. I continue quoting:
I am happy to say that these preliminary stages, inevitable and elaborate as they are but still only preliminary, have been passed. Fifty-two new firms have been offered contracts for the supply of ammunition, and of those fifty-two firms, at any rate up to ten days or a fortnight ago, fourteen have accepted term contracts.
Then he goes on to say that in developing this policy other companies must be still further trained, and points out that it is impossible to have what we call competitive

Bren Gun-Mr. Gardiner
bids in connection with a business of this kind; that in times of peace a government has to allow for reasonable profits in connection with contracts of this sort. Draft heads of contracts must be drawn to meet different situations, and by that process they get the production of their munitions and machinery of war.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if in 1936 I went to England convinced that government ownership and control of a plant in this country for the production of munitions would be a good thing under certain circumstances, I came back convinced that the British had had far more experience in this matter than we; that they found themselves confronted with a world situation which required them to develop the production of the machinery and munitions of war in the ordinary factories throughout the country, and that in order to get that done, they had to go into those plants, educate some of the staffs, reequip some of the plants with machinery and set up facilities by means of which the munitions of war could be produced. And that is what they did.
Some of my hon. friends opposite have been shouting to this government that we should show closer cooperation with the old country; that we should coordinate our efforts more closely with theirs. Here is one opportunity of coordinating our efforts without doing any injury to the national feelings, or to the feelings of any particular section of this dominion, and, while coordinating our efforts with theirs, we have an opportunity to develop our own industry so that in more peaceful times than we are enjoying at present we can go on to greater and greater development here.
Not so very long ago I said somewhere in this country-not while I was making a speech by the way, but while I was sitting at a table talking to a group of individuals- that what we wanted in Canada to-day if we were going to bring British settlers here from the industrial areas of England, was the transfer of some of the capital of Great Britain to this dominion. Immediately my hon. friends, particularly those over in the far corner on the opposite side, thought of capital as something in the form of money, something you could pick up and carry round with you. But the capital of the industrial areas of England is the machinery of production and the buildings that have been constructed to house that machinery. That machinery and those buildings, Mr. Speaker, represent the surplus labour of generations of Britishers who have established the industrial sections of that country. What I say is this, that
when we are faced with great difficulties such as those that are present in the world to-day; when we are faced with great threats such as we have in the world to-day, it is time to take advantage of our opportunities, and, while taking advantage of our opportunities, to give assistance to the industrial centre of the empire by seeing to it that some of these industries are carried on in Canada; for in carrying them on here we shall be transporting to this dominion not only the people who carry on those industries, but also the capital that has been built up through generations. By that method we can bring the men and women who are going to eat the foodstuffs of this country right to tie areas where those foodstuffs are being produced; we can put them to work developing our natural resources, instead of going on generation after generation supplying the needs of 30,000,000 industrial people from a country with only 10,000,000, located hundreds of miles away, and then wondering why there are threats of war from the thickly populated areas of this world.
This government entered into a joint contract with the British government to make guns which are needed by both governments, in one of the great cities of Canada where unemployment has been rife and where men are looking for work. My opposition friends who have been shouting, in Toronto more than anywhere else, that what we need is more cooperation with Great Britain, have seen one of their leading periodicals publish an article which insinuates all kinds of things. I say "insinuate" advisedly. I have had some experience with this periodical. On one occasion they wrote one of these insinuating articles with regard to me; inside an hour after it appeared on the news stands of my home city it was taken off the news stands, and my friends who publish this particular periodical took the trouble to send me the man who wrote it. He came half way across Canada to see me to find out what was wrong with it. When he came into my office and asked me what was wrong with it, I said, "There isn't anything wrong with it; I got more publicity out of this article than I ever got out of anything that was written about me in my life. I have found for the first time how many friends I have in my own city." Before that magazine had been on the news stands for an hour men were telephoning my office to ask me if I had read Maclean's magazine. I thought Maclean's magazine had really published something which was worth reading. I said, "No, I really do not waste much time reading
Bren Gun-Mr. Gardiner

it." "Well," they said, "you ought not to read it to-night because it says some terrible things about you, and we have put it off our news stands." This came from men who were not political friends of mine but who had read the article, as well as from friends. Having had that experience, I suggest to this house that this periodical is insinuating again, insinuating about the Minister of Defence {Mr. Mackenzie)-I do not know why-insinuating with regard to Major Hahn, who has entered into this contract. Let us look at what the commission's report says about Major Hahn. Not knowing Major Hahn, I can say freely what I am about to say. If hon. members will turn to page 12 of the report they will find some remarks in regard to him. I have not time to read all of these, but I want hon. members to read this. The deputy minister said, at page 15:
Major Hahn, he said, had come in to see him to ascertain whether there was any business which the department was giving and in which he might be interested.
It is interesting to note that this was on *October 9. It is also worth noting that the evidence shows that this plant was arranged for by Major Hahn in July and August of that year. On October 9 he called at the office of the deputy minister.
Major Hahn, he said, had come in to see him to ascertain whether there was any business which the department was giving and in which he might be interested. He mentioned aircraft, the possibility of making aircraft, and making shells or military equipment.
It appears that Major Hahn did not go there to get the contract for the Bren gun. He went there to make general inquiries from the department as to whether there was anything he could make that the department required. I have no doubt that a great many men have done that. The gentleman who got the letter of introduction through the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) came there to make the same kind of inquiry. Well then, the question in the evidence is:

A. Yes, very much.

On seeing the gun both of them (Mr. Plaxton and Major Hahn) went over to it, looked at it and asked what it was. I told them it was the new Bren gun. I do not believe that either of them had ever seen the gun."

munitions would cost from $30,000,000 to $35,000,000. I should like to read the paragraph in the report; it follows:
The minister said that General Ashton (the then chief of the general staff) was very insistent upon the development of government arsenals and that the former chief of general staff, General McNaughton, evolved a very comprehensive scheme for Valcartier which would include practically all the requirements of the Canadian forces.
The minister did not mention this when he was talking about the plant that wras purchased. I looked into the report and I found that what would cost between $30,000,000 and $35,000,000 was a comprehensive scheme which would include the manufacture of all the requirements of the forces. That did not refer in any way to the Bren gun contract, unless it were proposed to manufacture the Bren gun in that plant. The next paragraph in the report states that a new plant, apart from the land, would cost approximately $120,000. That is not $30,000,000 or $35,000,000. I think the minister is unfair to give out a statement like that and not state what the $30,000,000 to $35,000,000 are for. What is going on in Toronto at the John Inglis plant? I know the plant quite well, for I have been in it hundreds of times.

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) wants to say anything, he can say it later. He has a pretty sharp and witty tongue. I do not care what he wants to say, but I should not be interrupted while I am speaking. You can say any mortal thing you want to say about me. I have nothing to hide. I am not mixed up with any government contract and I am not defending anybody. My hon. friend is ready to defend anyone who comes to him for defence. I have such a high regard for his ability to defend people that if I ever got in trouble I would ask him to defend me if he wrere free.
The minister said something about British plants. When I was in England two years ago I visited a number of plants and I discussed with the officials the very point raised by the Minister of Agriculture. While there I listened to a debate in the House of Commons in connection with the removal of certain plants adjacent to London which were engaged in the manufacture of munitions. In Slough and other districts adjacent to London many plants had been erected and it was thought advisable that some of them should be moved farther away from London. I suggested to some of these officials that perhaps they could erect new plants in Canada. I may say to the minister that a number of these men told me that if any scheme could be worked out whereby a new plant could be erected in Canada and the necessary trading arrangements made, they would be glad to do it. As he and everybody else knows, they are moving their plants

Bren Gun-Mr. MacNicol
not only outside London but away north of Birmingham, and some of them have been moved north into Scotland. I think it would be a good scheme to induce British manufacturers to move out into this country. I would much rather have done that than induce three or four men, without a plant, and without machinery to operate a plant, to tiy to manufacture the Bren gun. I would have tried to encourage the manufacturers of the Enfield arms to build a branch plant here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is what we are doing not exactly what they were doing?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
You did not do it. You got hold of a man who made radios and got him to go into the armament business.
The Minister of Agriculture referred to my giving a letter of introduction to the Minister of National Defence. I would not hesitate two seconds to give a man dealing in wheat or flour a letter of introduction to the Minister of Agriculture. If every member of this house who has written a letter of introduction to a minister were asked by you, Mr. Speaker, to rise in his place, three-quarters of the membership of this house would have to rise. There is no crime in that, and I do not want any wrong inference to be drawn from that side of the house from the letter of introduction I wrote for John T. Hepburn.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I assure my hon. friend that there was not the slightest inference in the world with respect to himself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Thank you. I would expect a brother Scot to say that.
I want to deal now with two or three other matters. The company with which I was associated for a great many years bought a great number of boilers from the John Inglis plant, and I can say from my knowledge of the John Inglis plant that it was a fine plant for engines and boilers and heavy steelware. The Inglis family were a fine family, and it grieves me to see the Inglis name, which has meant so much in the city of Toronto for so long a time, dragged into an affair like this.
I knew the father, John Inglis, and I knew Mr. William Inglis who died, I think it was in 1935. They were very, very fine men, and it is a grief to every man who knew that family to have their name dragged into this affair, and as an old friend of the family, I am very, very sorry that the company which has taken over the plant was permitted to use the name Inglis. Give it any other name than the highly respectable name of Inglis. I am not saying that those who took it over were
not respectable; but the Inglis name had a fine record, and I never like to see an old established name like that used for any other purpose.
Something has been said about plants not being asked to tender for manufacturing the Bren gun. This afternoon, when my leader was speaking, he asked the Minister of National Defence if he denied that other manufacturers could make the Bren gun, and the minister replied, "Certainly not." I too would say, "Certainly not." I have been connected with the iron and steel business for many years and know a great many men who are in that business, making all kinds of precision tools and machinery that requires the finest of tools and the finest of mechanics, and I could name without hesitation many firms which could manufacture the Bren gun. When I was home on Saturday I took the trouble to ask two firms if they could manufacture the Bren gun. I do not want to mention their names, but I asked them if they could make the gun in their plant or on their property. They are both well known, reliable firms making various lines of machinery that require precision tools, and both answered without hesitation: Yes, they could have done so. That is one of the things I find fault with about this contract. It was given without tenders being invited, and at least twenty companies which could have made the Bren gun were not invited to tender at all. I have no doubt that when the Minister of National Defence rises to speak he will give his reasons why tenders were not invited. But speaking as a business man, engaged in large business for twenty-five years,
I would say that at least twenty companies could have made the Bren gun with some alterations in their plants. It is not necessary for me to read their names.
I know that the minister's department two or three years ago made an exhaustive survey of the industrial plants throughout Canada, and there is to-day in the department a compilation of their equipment and capacity, and what use could be made of these plants for military purposes. That report has been referred to several times since it appeared in the press on November 2, 1938, and I shall not take time to refer to it in more detail here.
I want to say a word or two on the method of letting tenders on a cost-plus basis. I do not approve it. I have had a great deal to do with business in my time, and I have always objected to having anything done on a cost-plus basis. I venture to say that in the Inglis plant in Toronto or in any plant where some' thing is being manufactured on a cost-plus basis you will find people falling over one
Bren Gun-Mr. MacNicol

another. The cost-plus basis just invites adding to the cost of the article; but let your contract by tender and you get a right price.
I am going to tabulate, in chronological order, the various items referred to in the commissioner's report, so that the whole Bren gun business will be plain for all who wish to read.
On May 24, 1935, the British government made an agreement with the patentee of the Bren gun, whose plant was established, I believe, in Czechoslovakia.
In August, 1935-I have not the precise date-two Bren guns were ordered shipped to Canada, according to the report.
On February 27, 1936, the high commissioner in London advised this government that, with regard to the agreement that had been entered into, Canada herself might manufacture the Bren gun, but if the Bren gun were made over here, she should take particular care to see that the gun was made in a plant operated by this government. That is one point which I should like kept firmly in mind, and it is brought up again and again in this report, that the Bren gun, if made here, must be manufactured by the government under its own supervision.
On March 18, 1936, the director of mechanization asked the judge advocate to study the agreement for Canada.
On March 19, 1936, the judge advocate replied.
On April 6, 1936, the John Inglis Company went into liquidation, and now commences the long story of the John Inglis Company.
The report says that late in March or early in April, 1936-it must have been early in April-Messrs. Cameron and Herbert and Gordon Plaxton were considering the Inglis plant, with a view, I suppose, to purchasing it.
On April 22, 1936, Major General Ashton wrote re the Bren gun and pointed out that the gun would have to be manufactured according to the agreement in a plant operated by the government.
On June 3, 1936, the Department of National Defence set its requirements at 7,000 Bren guns.
In June, 1936-the precise date is not given in the report-Mr. Herbert Plaxton interested Major Hahn in a proposal to acquire the Inglis plant, which was then in the hands of the receiver.
In July or August, it does not appear which, Major Hahn decided to become interested in the Inglis plant, with Messrs. Cameron, Pointon, Merritt, and Herbert and Gordon Plaxton.
[Mr. MacNicol.1
In August, 1936, Lieutenant Jolley returned from England. Lieutenant Jolley is an able man and I like what the report says about him. I like the way in which the Minister of Agriculture spoke about him. When it became necessary to send a man to England, why therefore did the government not send Lieutenant Jolley instead of Major Hahn and some others?
On August 24, 1936, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a letter which has been quoted and which, therefore, I shall not quote again. The Prime Minister replied on September 12 and was cautious, as he should be. He went to considerable pains to point out to the hon. member for Trinity that certain methods should be followed. But I was very much surprised to read in the report that on September 15, after receiving the Prime Minister's letter of September 12, the hon. member for Trinity sent the letter to the Minister of National Defence.
On October 9, the report records that the hon. member for Trinity and Major Hahn met in the deputy minister's office and, while there, saw the Breh gun.
On October 10 the department very wisely sent an inspector to investigate the Inglis plant. At that time the department must have had a full report with reference to that plant, because such a report must have been sent in by the inspectors who had been authorized to inspect all plants in Canada.
On October 19 Major Hahn, Mr. Cameron and the hon. member for Trinity saw the minister.
On October 19, it does not say whether before or after that visit, an offer was made by Messrs. Cameron, Pointon, and Merritt to buy the Inglis plant. The offer was to acquire the plant for $250,000 and that was accepted by the Toronto General Trust, I presume on the same date.
On October 19 the minister gave his letter of introduction to Major Hahn, and on October 20 the deputy minister also gave a letter of introduction.
On October 22, Mr. Nurse declared that the interest he held in the Inglis plant as trustee for J. D. Cameron, Herbert Plaxton and others was transferred into a new company capitalized at $1,200,000.
On October 23 the chief aeronautical officer reported in reference to the Inglis plant. What does he say about this plant? It has been quoted before but I think it should be

Bren Gun-Mr. MacNicol
read again. It will be found on page 22 of the report. He says in reference to this firm:
This firm is equipped to do heavy engineering work, boilers, etc. The shops would require to be stripped of their equipment to be suitable for aircraft construction. The shops are more suitable for shells, gun carriage, etc., than for aircraft or aircraft engines.
I know that during the great war the Inglis company did make a vast number of shells for shipment overseas.
On October 26 Major Hahn, the hon. member for Trinity and Mr. Gordon Plaxton sailed for England.
On November 9, the hon. member for Trinity sent two cables from England, one to the minister and one to the deputy. As they have both been read I shall not quote them again.
On November 10 the cables were replied to, making Major Hahn representative of the government.
On November 16 the Anglo-Engineering Company was incorporated to hold some shares of the John Inglis Company.
On November 23 the British Engineering Company was incorporated, having 200,000 shares of one dollar each.
Having been associated with an old-line company that had been in business since 1884, and having customers from one end of the country to the other, I am perfectly at a loss to understand why there should be any necessity whatever for the incorporation of all these companies for the making of the Bren machine guns.
On March 5, 1937, an interdepartmental committee was set up.
On June 4 the company's name was changed to the John Inglis Company. That is something which I very much regret, and I say so in view of the fact that this was an old-established firm and one that was highly respected.
On December 17 another company was set up, Investment Reserves Incorporated, to act as trustees for certain shares in the John Inglis Company.
On January 5, 1937, the interdepartmental committee met to discuss the Inglis contract.
On January 13, a subcommittee of the interdepartmental committee made a report. What did they say? At page 38 of the report this statement appears, that various other companies might have made this equipment, or should have been asked for bids on the equipment; and they discussed the subject of competitive bids, the question why the
John Inglis Company should get this contract, the financial status of the company, and a number of other things. Now that is what the public wants to know. The people want to know why only one company was allowed to have the privilege of manufacturing these guns, especially a company that was not in the business, certainly not in the manufacturing business. They might have been getting ready to manufacture, but they were not actually doing so.
On January 24 the interdepartmental committee discussed the question why other companies were not invited to tender.
On March 22 the contract was authorized, and on March 31 the contract was signed. On April 1 the plant commenced operating.
That is the chronological order as far as I have been able to trace it from the report, giving the various dates of the transaction. The Minister of Agriculture made reference to the Ross rifle, and that recalled to my mind what I heard in Toronto on Saturday last from a man who has two sons who, in the event of war, would likely enlist or be enrolled in the forces. This gentleman said to me: "I am horrified to think what might happen to my sons because I have a clear recollection of what happened in connection with the Ross rifle in the great war." As the Minister of Agriculture said, soldiers threw that rifle away. As we read at that time, a great number of Canadian soldiers lost their lives through the inefficiency of the Ross rifle. What assurance is there to-day that the Bren will be worth a fig? At the time the Ross rifles were made, the Ross rifle factory at Quebec was supposed to be equipped with the finest machinery, but apparently it was not able to turn out guns which were reliable. What assurance is there that the Bren guns made in the old John Inglis plant will be any better? They would perhaps, however, be too heavy for the soldiers to throw away. I hope these guns will be efficient; I trust they will, but what assurance have we that they will be any better manufactured than the old Ross rifles were? That is a question that disturbs the people of the city from which I come.
I appreciate the fact that the government gave the contract, when it did give it, to a plant in Toronto. I am one of those who firmly believe that everything that can be made in this country should be so made; I know there were at least a score of plants in Canada at that time which could have gone into making Bren guns without too much change, companies with which I am well acquainted myself. So that the government
Bren Gun-Mr. Pelletier

has to answer that question why one company only, and that one apparently organized on purpose to make Bren guns, was given the opportunity to tender on the Bren gun, to the exclusion of several old-established companies.

speechtext:
This debate has arisen on a motion by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Mac-Neil) that the Bren gun investigation report should be referred to the standing committee on public accounts. When the motion was made the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke on it; since then many other members of the government have also spoken, and they all insist that they have carefully read the report and found absolutely nothing wrong. If that be the case they must have been wearing rose-coloured glasses when they read it, because it is evident from the report that there certainly are things which need correction in connection with this matter. I am surprised at the attitude taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). He began by saying that in his opinion the commissioner had been limited in several ways in making his report. For example, he continuously referred to parts of the report quoting arguments presented by various counsel. For example, Mr. Geoffrion, counsel for one of the parties concerned, said to the commissioner :
No charges being laid, no report of misconduct or no report can be made against us, because there was no charge of misconduct, and no notice to us . . . and I say on the record, as it is now made, it is completely ultra vires, and it is of course inconceivable that there should be a report of misconduct, as there has been no charge.
He also said:
Under the circumstances, so far as Major Hahn and the John Inglis Company are concerned, I suggest-and I suggest this most emphatically-that there is absolutely no jurisdiction in finding misconduct of any sort on his part.
But the subject of public concern is, in my opinion, that at the conclusion of a long hearing. counsel in their arguments, except counsel for Colonel Drew, raised all sorts of objections to the commissioner commenting on the evidence, or expressing any opinion that he might see fit to express, or making any recommendation as a result of his investigation, although he was expressly directed by his commission to do so. Further on we find this statement by Mr. Geoffrion to the commissioner :
You can report the facts, but if the facts of the report necessarily involve a charge of misconduct, you cannot.

It seems to me that the meaning of the word "misconduct" certainly has something to do with the interpretation which the commissioner might place on the argument of counsel. If misconduct simply means that there is something directly wrong with the minister or with the contract, it is possible that the commissioner could not have looked into it from that particular angle. But if misconduct means that perhaps the negotiations leading to the letting of the contract were not conducted as they should have been, then it is my opinion that the commissioner should not have been influenced by the argument of counsel. There is, however, no evidence that he was. But I feel inclined to ask this question:	In view of the fact that this
statement was repeated to the commissioner so many times by various people appearing before him as counsel, is it possible to believe that the commissioner felt there were certain questions which, in the light of representations made by counsel, he should not ask? I doubt that, however, because the commissioner has stated that the inquiry was open. But in the light of the arguments presented by the leader of the opposition I fail to see why he should not be willing to let the matter go to the committee.
The other day the Prime Minister said something in connection with what might be the rights of hon. members if this investigation were put before a select committee of the house. I admit that at that time the words of the Prime Minister seemed to put a certain restraint upon hon. members of this house.
I felt that if I went ahead and spoke in this debate regardless of the words of the Prime Minister, perhaps I should be exceeding what would be considered proper by him. I recalled, however, that perhaps the Prime Minister was following the tactics sometimes used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) who at times rises in his place and thunders at the house, telling hon. members what dire things will happen to them if such and such a course of action is followed. As a case in point, I should like to quote a few lines from Hansard to show the attitude that is sometimes taken by the Minister of Finance, which perhaps influenced the stand taken by the Prime Minister the other day. In 1938 we find the Minister of Finance, in an endeavour, I imagine, to compel some hon. members to realize the dire danger of some things which they were doing, thundering out these words, as reported at page 474 of Hansard for February 15, 1938: May I point out that in an authoritarian state a man who said what the leader of the opposition said would by now be in another

Bren Gun-Mr. Pelletier
sphere; he would have been "liquidated" or- what is the other word?-"purged." As for my hon. friend from Peace River (Hr. Pelletier) what would have happened to him I shudder to think.
Remembering the words of the Minister of Finance I thought the Prime Minister was perhaps following in his footsteps and in that manner trying to tell us not to do something which he felt should not be done.
I listened with great care to the argument of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that someone in this house was criticizing Major Hahn. As far as I am concerned I am not worrying about Major Hahn, but in the light of the report on the Bren machine gun the question that concerns u's is what will happen to the money which shortly will be in the hands of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), if such things as this are permitted to go on. True, no one has found any corruption of any kind; no one has ever suggested any corruption, but I am sure we are all agreed that the method by which this contract was negotiated is not a method which should be followed in a democratic country. That is the point at stake, rather than the reputation of Major Hahn or anybody else, and I submit that when the Minister of Agriculture dwelt on that point he failed to touch the argument at all. The minister also referred to the inference left by the leader of the opposition-of course according to the minister-

speechtext: Look at the paper.
