speechtext:
Yes; I will look at the paper and get it right. The minister referred to the inference left by the leader of the opposition during the course of his speech. I suggest that if there were any such inference, it was no worse than the inference suggested by the leader of the government himself when he referred to the political affiliations of the judge appointed to conduct the inquiry. It seemed to me that when the Prime Minister stated that this judge was not of Liberal origin or appointed by the Liberal party, that he was a Conservative, it must have meant to the people at large that some doubt must be reflected upon those who had been appointed under a Liberal administration. It did not seem to me that the Prime Minister should have made any such reference, because it does cast some sort of reflection upon the Supreme Court of Canada. I have always felt that once men have been appointed to such exalted positions, they leave behind all their political partisanship and become solely interested in justice, no matter who may be concerned.
71492-44 J
It might be well to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the gentleman who was retained as counsel for one of the interested parties, namely Mr. Geoffrion, is the gentleman who last year was engaged by this government to present the case of the federal government to the Supreme Court of Canada in the matter of the reference of certain statutes of the province of Alberta. This is probably simply a coincidence, but I mention it in passing because I feel that it might be a good thing if it were more widely known.
In my opinion the purpose of this debate is not simply to find fault with any minister of the government but to make sure, by referring the matter to a properly constituted committee of this house, that we in Canada may be absolutely sure that there is no tinkering, shall I say, with anything having to do with the question of munitions or the awarding of contracts. Probably the Prime Minister remembers very well what occurred in this house last year during the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The then leader of the opposition made certain charges having to do with graft and political corruption. I said he made charges, but I should have said he made insinuations. At that time I suggested to the leader of the government that perhaps it would be best to ask the leader of the opposition to prove those charges and thus clear the atmosphere. There might not have been anything to them, and perhaps the whole thing would have died away. I believe if that course had been followed, such occurrences as we are discussing to-day might not have taken place.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I admit, of course, that this investigation does not concern any scandal, but the very fact that a committee had investigated political patronage naturally would have tended to restrain the ministers from considering granting favours to certain political friends. I agree with the Minister of Agriculture when he says Major Hahn simply sold himself to the Department of National Defence. Of course he sold himself, with the assistance of one of the supporters of this government. That was the way in which the thing was done, and perhaps if my suggestion last year had been adopted this situation would not have arisen.
I know very well it is the desire of the Prime Minister to have absolute integrity on the part of his government and to have nothing wrong with any contract dealing with

Bren Gun-Mr. Pelletier
the question of armaments for this country. In this connection I submit the following for his consideration; the commissioner made the following recommendation:
Wliat is plain to me at the end of this long inquiry is this: that if the policy of private manufacture of wa r munitions and armaments is to be continued in this country (a question of administrative policy for the government and parliament to determine), once the requirements are determined by the Department of National Defence the negotiations leading up to and the making of contracts between the government and private manufacturers either for the purchase or production of such munitions or armaments should be put into the hands of an expert advisory group of competent business men-a capable and experienced manufacturer, a commercial lawyer who has had a wide practice in dealing with large commercial contracts, a representative of labour, and say a chartered accountant who has had experience in the examination of substantial business transactions. These persons should constitute a board (which might be known as the "Defence Purchasing Board") -
Knowing as I do the sincere, earnest desire of the Prime Minister to bring about such a happy situation, I suggest that it would be a wonderful gesture on his part if he were to arrange to have such a board properly constituted and to have it report not only to the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance but also to the leader of the opposition and to another member representing the independent groups in this house. Handled in that way, with such an open-handed gesture, I feel sure that this question of political patronage in connection with contracts would never again arise in this country. That is simply a suggestion; I realize that it might not be advisable from the point of view of the government, but I believe at a time like this the government would be quite willing to put aside questions of party and rise to greater heights for the sake of the economic welfare of the Canadian people. I feel confident that if such a plan were accepted by the Prime Minister, it would at once remove all doubt in the minds of the people of Canada in regard to the handling of matters of this kind. There is no doubt that to-day many people are questioning themselves and others with regard to what is happening in connection with contracts of this kind. People are too prone to go around the country saying, "Oh, sure, somebody is making money out of this thing, and we have to pay for it in taxation, or perhaps with the lives of our sons or husbands." It is only right that they should ask themselves such questions, when they read the report of the Nye committee of the United States senate. Anyone interested in this question of the private manufacture of munitions will find a great deal of interesting reading in that report. No doubt 
that question will be discussed by the committee, and perhaps a recommendation will be made that there should be no private gain in the manufacture of armaments. That I do not know; nevertheless one cannot help but be struck by words such as these, from the report of the committee to which I just referred:
*-it is clear that the private shipbuilders should very definitely be policed in any and all moves made by them or through them to confuse public defence needs with their private profit, or should be cut off entirely from the building of ships for the navy.
Of course this part of the report refers particularly to the navy, the shipyards, the building of battleships and cruisers, and armaments of that kind. But armaments are armaments no matter whether they are Bren machine guns or boats, and the people never like to make that kind of expenditure unless they feel it is absolutely necessary. That is why I say to the Prime Minister that if he were to follow, perhaps with certain modifications, the suggestion which I have made, he would at once remove from the minds of the people of this country any thought that there might be anything wrong with the handling of contracts of this kind.
Undoubtedly we shall have occasion later on to refer once more to the findings of this commission, when the report comes from the committee to which it is intended it shall be referred. I believe that nothing is to be lost by referring this report to the committee. I cannot agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that the debate arising out of the report has finally cleared the atmosphere. In my mind too many doubts have been raised to be left where they are; they need to be cleared up; and I feel that the only possible place to clear them up is where members of a committee have free access to all documents and have the power to bring before them any person whom they may see fit to call. I repeat this because there may have been the thought in the mind of the commissioner that he was precluded by a section of the Inquiries Act from asking certain questions which otherwise he might have asked.
I conclude these few words in the hope that the Prime Minister will give serious consideration to the suggestion that I have made, because I believe that only by rising above political lines shall we be able to retain the confidence of the people of this country with regard to armament manufacture.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read the report and I believe the people have read it. I can come to only one conclusion, that we should have the full discus-

Bren Gun-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
sion on this matter which we are having. The people demand a full discussion right on the floor of this house, not in any committee. I do not want to take any chances of having discussion blocked by technicalities. We want to have the scope of discussion as wide as possible.
The impassioned speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made on this motion sounded to me, a new member, like intimidation. I am sure some other hon. members felt the same way, but I can assure him that I am not intimidated. He said, as reported at page 596 of Hansard:
What I am concerned about is that some other hon. members in the course of debate at this stage may without realizing the significance of their actions commit themselves by their expressions to such an extent that every man, woman and child in this country will know that they have arrived at a particular attitude which they intend to maintain in the committee, and that the committee therefore would lose in the public mind if not also in fact the judicial aspect which it ought to have.
I do not believe the discussion will lose any judicial aspect if it is conducted on the floor of this house. What I am more concerned about is that if this contract is referred to a committee which will be composed of some thirty-six members of the government and only fourteen members from other parts of the house, every man, woman and child will not know the facts. The Prime Minister knows he need have no fear, because before this discussion is over every man, woman and child in this country will know the facts and will be able to judge for themselves whether this contract is good or bad.
There is no need to refer this contract to any committee. It is bad. Anyone reading the report and studying it knows it is bad. It should be cancelled. Any man of the ability of the Prime Minister knows it is bad. Why refer it to the public accounts committee? "Why go to the expense of a further investigation? The facts are all before us in the report. The evidence is there. Why not now cancel the contract? Is the Prime Minister not apprehensive about its being carried out? If he is, he had better cancel it. What about the cost of production? Suppose we examine for a few minutes the stock set-up of the company. I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that 250,000 shares are issued to the John Inglis Company at $6 a share. That amounts to $1,500,000, made up as follows:

at $6	$349,998

What did they pay for these 191,662 shares? They paid $100,000, or a little more than fifty-two cents a share. Some treasury stock was sold for $231,000, at between $6 and $750. Nevertheless Major Hahn and his associates paid only a little more than fifty-two cents. The profit on the transaction, at $6 a share, was $1,049,972. If we take into account that they had to pay $100,000 for that stock and they made that profit, it was given them for the Bren gun contract.
It has been argued that it would be very costly for the government to undertake this contract. Yet all the real cash it was proposed to carry on with was the proceeds of the treasury stock, between three and four hundred thousand dollars, plus the $100,000 cash, or about $500,000. The argument that it would be too costly for the government to carry out this contract does not hold good, because it would cost them only $500,000 plus what they have put into it, and if the government had taken the contract themselves they would have saved the $1,149,972 which these other fellows are going to get. I shall speak again about that a little later.
Did the Prime Minister instruct counsel? He said he did, according to a press report. Who employs counsel? The Prime Minister. Who should instruct counsel? The Prime Minister. He asked if it was his duty. He should not need to ask; he should know. Possibly he will appoint another commission to tell him whether he should instruct counsel. On page 50 of his report Mr. Justice Davis states:
The question is: Were proper and sufficient steps taken in this case to discharge that responsibility? Upon the whole evidence, that is a question for the government and parliament to pass upon.
He says that is a question for the government and parliament to pass upon. That object can be attained only by full discussion without limit as to scope. The public are demanding it, and they are entitled to it. How were the individual firms or corporations selected? Were they selected as a result of a departmental investigation? I quote from page 2912 of Hansard of May 16, 1938, as follows:
Some eighteen months ago an industrial survey was commenced under the direction of the master general of the ordnance. Speaking in round figures, I believe about 700 firms in various parts of Canada have been surveyed with reference to their potential capacity for production in any particular direction in the event of a national emergency.
That is a statement by the minister. If the Inglis company were picked out as a result of this investigation by the ordnance branch, then it is an insult to the abilities,

Bren Gun-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
the capacities and reputations of the 700 firms investigated. I cannot think for one minute that the ordnance branch could have been so inefficient as to place the John Inglis Company at the head of the list of 700 odd firms which had been investigated. If they did, then we certainly need a clean-up in the ordnance branch. These are days of national emergency. What is the use of investigating 700, 800 or a thousand firms and then pigeonholing the investigation? That is something I cannot understand. Perhaps that will come out in the discussion on the floor of this house. This plant was inspected in October, 1936, at the request of the deputy minister. I quote from page 22 of the report as follows:
This plant is primarily equipped for the manufacture of boilers, turbines and the working of heavy plate generally.
I ask hon. members if the Bren gun resembles a turbine or a boiler, or if heavy plate is used in its manufacture? I quote:
... it might be used for the manufacture of tanks or shells.
Does the Bren gun look like a tank or a shell? I do not think it does. This plant was not the best plant in Canada. What are the main requisites for the manufacture of the precision parts in a piece of mechanism like the Bren gun? They are knowledge, experience and skilled workmen. Did the Inglis company have any of these? I quote again from page 22 of the report:
This factory is at present inoperative and has not been in operation since April, 1936. There is no design staff at present employed and the total number of workmen now employed consists of three men as factory maintenance staff.
These are the workmen and this is the equipment which formed part of this fully equipped factory or factories which were controlled by Major Hahn and his group. These are the factories which were chosen to manufacture this piece of precision mechanism. The deputy minister said that they had surveyed nearly a thousand plants. I submit that that survey of a thousand plants was disregarded entirely. Why was that survey disregarded? That is something which parliament should find out. I quote a question and an answer reported on page 29 of the report as follows:
Q. But there were firms in Canada who had been doing very delicate steel operations for a great many years, were there not?
A. In my judgment it had nothing whatsoever to do with the question, because for this reason, that any company in Canada could not undertake this particular contract unless there was a greater volume of production to reduce the cost of production-and that was essentially a vital factor in the whole thing.

That was the minister's judgment. He said that any company in Canada could not undertake this particular contract unless there were a greater volume of production to reduce the cost of production. It would be too expensive. How ridiculous it is to talk about the cost of producing these guns and the cost of putting up a plant! The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) certainly left in some of our minds an impression that it was going to cost some $30,000,000 or $35,000,000, or possibly $200,000,000, in his judgment. What was to happen to all the money that was to come from the promotion of the sale of this stock? Was there: to be profiteering? All they paid for the 191,662 shares which they got was a little over fifty-two cents per share. What was paid for the treasury shares which were sold to the public? The public paid between $6 and $7. Did they not have in their minds that these 191,662 shares would go up in value? Do you think they were not looking for profit? Not only did they get these 191,662 shares, but as time goes on those shares might be worth $10, $15, or even $20 each. Is that making armaments for this country without profit? The minister gave his judgment with respect' to the cost of production and stated that was why he did not ask other firms to do the job. How did he know what the cost of production was going to be? None of these firms had a chance to bid on the Bren gun contract. None of them was asked.
It may be said that possibly some of these firms would not go into production unless they got a big profit, but when I was home over the weekend I took the trouble to go round to several of these firms. Again I do not wish to mention names, but I was assured that if the manufacture of armaments in Canada were necessary, and if it was put up to them, they would manufacture armaments at a very small profit. They also felt that the manufacture of these armaments would be just as much for their own benefit as for the benefit of all the rest of the community. They would be willing to enter into contracts. They would get a group together to manufacture Bren guns, and they would not be paying out profits by way of stock promotion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A million dollars profit by way of stock promotion! Parliament has to find out why these firms were not approached. There is a great deal in this report about why they were not approached, but I think we need to know a little more about it. The great thing to-day

Bren Gun-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
is that this country needs these guns. The minister himself says that they are of vital necessity to Canada. I am sure that if this contract were cancelled, there would be no difficulty at all in getting the manufacturers of this country together, telling them that there was an emergency and that guns were needed, and in having them manufacture all the guns that were needed. After all, Mr. Speaker, who is it that understands the manufacture of these things? Is it this gentleman who is a manufacturer of radios or refrigerators? What does he know about the heat- treatment of steel and alloys and precision steel down to the ten-thousandth of an inch? All he knows is no more than our young friend, Mr. Jolley, a graduate of my own university, knows, and Mr. Jolley is a good man. I know something about him, and he does know something about the manufacture of this stuff.
Canadian manufacturers are keen to manufacture all our defence requirements, and they do not want profits. They want to keep their workmen employed. We do not want profits out of armaments in this country. We do not want to make money out of blood. Our own manufacturers would do this job for you if you would only give them a chance, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that they have never had a chance. The Department of National Defence is responsible for that. I repeat, it is the Department of National Defence that is responsible.
I wish to quote further from the report with reference to the interdepartmental committee. That committee had somewhat the same ideas that I have expressed. They would have been able to find out the same sort of thing that I found out, and I am perfectly sure that they would have found that there would be no difficulty in getting our own manufacturers to make these guns. I know they could have got a group of manufacturers together to manufacture these guns, in a government-owned factory, if you like, and these manufacturers would give all the assistance that was necessary to the government to have these guns manufactured in Canada; but as long as we are going to have patronage in the manufacture of armaments in this country we are not going to get some manufacturers to sacrifice their chances, just at their own expense.
Let me quote from page 37 of the report:
We-
That is the interdepartmental committee:
We pointed out that there was a number of very substantial subsisting companies in Canada that were manufacturing precision tools, and had experience in what we thought was
this line of work. We felt that they should be consulted and given an opportunity to submit competitive tenders.
That is a pretty strong statement. I think it would take a great deal of persuasion to turn these men away from that attitude. They had evidently gone into this matter carefully, and they knew what their duty was with respect to the situation. They realized the seriousness of it. They are the highest type of men we have in Canada, and why was not their recommendation acted on? Why did somebody override them? What was the reason for their advice being disregarded? Parliament wants to know why. We do not want to take this thing into some committee, with a preponderance of government members, and be choked off, as so often happens in these committees, by technicalities being raised and things of that sort. We want a thorough discussion of the whole matter on the floor of this house, so that every man, woman and child in this country will know about these things. How can we ever expect our young men to enlist in the militia when they hear about this kind of thing; when they know this sort of thing is going on; when they know of the patronage that exists in the Department of National Defence? Look at the regiments in Toronto! How are they now? Away down below strength. How are they treated? They cannot get boots or anything at all. It is disgraceful. What an opportunity the Department of National Defence has to do something for these young fellows!
I see it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
